Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 1–6:

Surat al-Waqi'ah is Meccan, and it has ninety-seven verses. It is Meccan according to al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Jabir and 'Ata'. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: "Except for one verse of it, which was revealed in Medina, and it is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And you make your provision that you deny?﴾" Al-Kalbi said: "It is Meccan except for four verses, two of which (﴿Then is it at this discourse that you scoff?﴾ and ﴿And you make your provision that you deny?﴾) were revealed during his journey to Mecca, and His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿A throng of the earlier peoples, and a throng of the later peoples﴾ were revealed during his journey to Medina."

Masruq said: "Whoever wishes to know the news of the earlier and later peoples, and the news of the people of Paradise, and the news of the people of Hellfire, and the news of the people of this world, and the news of the people of the Hereafter, let him recite Surat al-Waqi'ah."

Abu 'Umar Ibn 'Abd al-Barr mentioned in (al-Tamhid) and (al-Ta'liq), and al-Tha'labi also, that 'Uthman entered upon Ibn Mas'ud to visit him during the illness from which he died. He said: "What do you complain of?" He said: "My sins." He said: "What do you desire?" He said: "The mercy of my Lord." He said: "Shall we not call a physician for you?" He said: "The physician has made me ill." He said: "Shall we not order your stipend to be given to you?" He said: "I have no need of it. You withheld it from me during my life, and you would give it to me at my death?" He said: "It will be for your daughters after you." He said: "Do you fear for my daughters poverty after me? I have commanded them to recite Surat (al-Waqi'ah) every night, for I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Whoever recites Surat al-Waqi'ah every night, poverty will never afflict him.'"

بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ

إِذا وَقَعَتِ الْواقِعَةُ (١) لَيْسَ لِوَقْعَتِها كاذِبَةٌ (٢) خافِضَةٌ رافِعَةٌ (٣) إِذا رُجَّتِ الْأَرْضُ رَجًّا (٤)

وَبُسَّتِ الْجِبالُ بَسًّا (٥) فَكانَتْ هَباءً مُنْبَثًّا (٦)

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿When the Inevitable Event occurs﴾, i.e., the Resurrection has come to pass, and what is meant is the final blast. It was called "the Event" (al-waqi'ah) because it will occur suddenly. It was also said: because of the great number of hardships that occur in it. There is an implied element here, i.e., "Remember when the Inevitable Event occurs." Al-Jurjani said: "(idha) is an extraneous element (silah), i.e., 'the Event occurs,' like His saying: (The Hour has drawn near) and (The command of Allah has come), and it is like saying: 'The fast has come,' meaning it has drawn near and approached. According to the first view, (idha) denotes a time, and its response is His saying: (Then the companions of the right hand—what are the companions of the right hand?)."

(﴿There is no denying its occurrence﴾) The word "kadhibah" is a verbal noun meaning "denial," and the Arabs sometimes place the active participle and the passive participle in the place of the verbal noun, as in His saying: (You will not hear in it any idle talk) [i.e., laghw], and the meaning is that no denial of it will be heard, as said by al-Kisa'i. From this comes the common saying: "'a'idhan billah," meaning "ma'adh Allah" (God forbid), and "qum qa'iman," meaning "qum qiyaman" (stand up). And one of the Arab women, lulling her son, said:

Stand up standing, stand up standing...
You have caught a sleeping slave.

It was also said: "al-kadhibah" is an adjective whose noun is omitted, meaning there is no state of its occurrence that is false, or no soul that is false, i.e., everyone who reports about its occurrence is truthful. Al-Zajjaj said: "(There is no denying its occurrence)" means nothing can repel it. Similar is the saying of al-Hasan and Qatadah. Al-Thawri said: there is no one who denies it. Al-Kisa'i also said: there is no denial of it, i.e., no one should deny it. It was also said: its establishment is a true matter, not a jest.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Bringing low, lifting up﴾. 'Ikrimah, Muqatil and al-Suddi said: it lowers the voice so that it makes those who are near hear, and raises those who are far, meaning it makes the near and the far hear. Al-Suddi said: it brings low the arrogant and raises up the oppressed. Qatadah said: it brings low peoples into the punishment of Allah, and raises up peoples to the obedience of Allah. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it brings low the enemies of Allah into the Fire, and raises up the friends of Allah into Paradise. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: it brings low peoples who were exalted in the world, and raises up peoples who were lowly in the world. Ibn 'Ata' said: it brings low some peoples by justice, and raises up others by grace. "Khafd" (lowering) and "raf'" (raising) are used in Arabic regarding place and rank, and honor and humiliation. Allah, glorified is He, attributed lowering and raising to the Resurrection figuratively and metaphorically, according to the Arabic habit of attributing an act to a place, a time, and other things that are not themselves the agent, as they say: "a sleeping night" and "a fasting day." In the revelation: (Rather, the plotting of the night and the day). The true bringer-low and raiser-up is Allah alone: He raises His friends to the highest ranks and brings low His enemies to the lowest depths. Al-Hasan and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read (khafidatun rafi'atun) in the accusative. The rest read it in the nominative, on the supposition of an omitted subject. Whoever reads it in the accusative does so as a circumstantial accusative (hal). According to al-Farra', it is on the supposition of an omitted verb, and the meaning is: "When the Inevitable Event occurs; there is no denying its occurrence—it occurs bringing low and lifting up." There is no doubt about the occurrence of the Resurrection, and that it raises some peoples and lowers others, as we have explained.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿When the earth is shaken with a shaking﴾, i.e., it is convulsed and moved, according to Mujahid and others. It is said: "rajjahu yarujjuhu rajjan," meaning he moved it and convulsed it. And "naqah rajja'" means one with a large hump. In a hadith: "Whoever boards the sea when it is agitated has no protection," meaning when its waves are turbulent. Al-Kalbi said: that is because when Allah reveals to it, it trembles out of fear of Allah, the Exalted. The exegetes said: it shakes as a child shakes in the cradle, until everything upon it collapses and everything upon it, from mountains and others, is shattered. Ibn 'Abbas said: the rajjah is a violent movement accompanied by a sound. The place of (idha) is in the accusative as a substitute for (idha waqa'at). It is also permissible for it to be governed by (khafidatun rafi'ah), meaning it lowers and raises at the time when the earth is shaken and the mountains are crumbled, because at that time what is high is lowered and what is low is raised. It was also said: the meaning is "The Event occurs when the earth is shaken," as said by al-Zajjaj and al-Jurjani. It was also said: meaning "Remember when the earth is shaken with a shaking," a verbal noun, which is evidence for the repetition of the earthquake.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And the mountains are crumbled to powder﴾, i.e., they are pulverized, according to Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: like flour is crumbled, i.e., kneaded. The "basisah" is toasted flour or meal kneaded with ghee or oil, then eaten without cooking, and it may be taken as provision. The rajiz said:

Do not bake bread and crumbled bread for us,
And do not prolong a halt in a dwelling of constriction.

Abu 'Ubaydah mentioned that he was a thief from Ghatafan who wanted to bake, but feared he would be hurried away from it, so he ate it as dough. The meaning is that they are mixed, becoming like flour kneaded with some water, i.e., the mountains become dust, so some part mixes with another. Al-Hasan said: "bussat" means they were uprooted from their base and went away, akin to His saying: (My Lord will scatter them as scattering). 'Ata'iyyah said: they were spread out like sand and dust. It was also said: "al-bass" means driving, i.e., the mountains are driven. Abu Zayd said: "al-bass" is driving; one says, "I drove the camels, abussuha, bassan." Abu 'Ubayd said: "bassata al-ibil" and "abassta" are two dialects, when you drive them and say to them "bis bis." In a hadith: "A people will go out from Medina to Yemen, Syria and Iraq, driving (yabussuna), and Medina is better for them, if they only knew." And from it another hadith: "The people of Yemen came to you driving their dependents (yabussuna 'iyalahum)." The Arabs say: "Bring it to you from your sensing (hassika) and your driving (bassika)." Abu Zayd transmitted both with a kasrah: "min hassika" means from where you perceived it, and "bassika" means from where your journey reached it. Mujahid said: it flowed as a flood. 'Ikrimah: it was demolished with demolition. Muhammad ibn Ka'b: it was set moving with movement, and from it is the saying of al-Aghlab al-'Ijli [a blank in the manuscripts at the place of the witness from the verse of al-Aghlab al-'Ijli the rajiz, and we have not found it]. Al-Hasan said: it was cut into pieces. The meanings are close.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿So they become scattered dust motes﴾. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "al-hala' al-munbath" is the dust (rahj) that rises from the hooves of animals and then disappears, and Allah made their deeds like that. Mujahid said: "al-habaʾ" is the ray that appears in a window like dust. Something similar is reported from Ibn 'Abbas. Also from him: it is what flies off from fire when it is agitated; sparks fly from it, and when it falls it is nothing. 'Ata'iyyah said likewise. It has passed in (al-Furqan) at His saying: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust motes﴾. The common reading is "munbathhan" with the three-dotted tha', meaning scattered, from His saying: ﴿And He scattered therein every creature﴾, i.e., He dispersed and spread them. Masruq, al-Nakha'i and Abu Haywah read "munbattan" with a two-dotted ta', meaning cut off, from the saying of people: "battahu Allah," i.e., He cut it off, and from it "al-battat."

Masruq, al-Nakha'i and Abu Haywah read "munbattan" with a two-dotted ta', meaning cut off, from the saying of people: "battahu Allah," i.e., He cut it off, and from it "al-battat."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 1–6:

Surat al-Waqi'ah is Meccan, and it has ninety-seven verses. It is Meccan according to al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Jabir and 'Ata'. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: "Except for one verse of it, which was revealed in Medina, and it is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And you make your provision that you deny?﴾" Al-Kalbi said: "It is Meccan except for four verses, two of which (﴿Then is it at this discourse that you scoff?﴾ and ﴿And you make your provision that you deny?﴾) were revealed during his journey to Mecca, and His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿A throng of the earlier peoples, and a throng of the later peoples﴾ were revealed during his journey to Medina."

Masruq said: "Whoever wishes to know the news of the earlier and later peoples, and the news of the people of Paradise, and the news of the people of Hellfire, and the news of the people of this world, and the news of the people of the Hereafter, let him recite Surat al-Waqi'ah."

Abu 'Umar Ibn 'Abd al-Barr mentioned in (al-Tamhid) and (al-Ta'liq), and al-Tha'labi also, that 'Uthman entered upon Ibn Mas'ud to visit him during the illness from which he died. He said: "What do you complain of?" He said: "My sins." He said: "What do you desire?" He said: "The mercy of my Lord." He said: "Shall we not call a physician for you?" He said: "The physician has made me ill." He said: "Shall we not order your stipend to be given to you?" He said: "I have no need of it. You withheld it from me during my life, and you would give it to me at my death?" He said: "It will be for your daughters after you." He said: "Do you fear for my daughters poverty after me? I have commanded them to recite Surat (al-Waqi'ah) every night, for I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Whoever recites Surat al-Waqi'ah every night, poverty will never afflict him.'"

بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ

بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ

إِذا وَقَعَتِ الْواقِعَةُ (١) لَيْسَ لِوَقْعَتِها كاذِبَةٌ (٢) خافِضَةٌ رافِعَةٌ (٣) إِذا رُجَّتِ الْأَرْضُ رَجًّا (٤)

وَبُسَّتِ الْجِبالُ بَسًّا (٥) فَكانَتْ هَباءً مُنْبَثًّا (٦)

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿When the Inevitable Event occurs﴾, i.e., the Resurrection has come to pass, and what is meant is the final blast. It was called "the Event" (al-waqi'ah) because it will occur suddenly. It was also said: because of the great number of hardships that occur in it. There is an implied element here, i.e., "Remember when the Inevitable Event occurs." Al-Jurjani said: "(idha) is an extraneous element (silah), i.e., 'the Event occurs,' like His saying: (The Hour has drawn near) and (The command of Allah has come), and it is like saying: 'The fast has come,' meaning it has drawn near and approached. According to the first view, (idha) denotes a time, and its response is His saying: (Then the companions of the right hand—what are the companions of the right hand?)."

(﴿There is no denying its occurrence﴾) The word "kadhibah" is a verbal noun meaning "denial," and the Arabs sometimes place the active participle and the passive participle in the place of the verbal noun, as in His saying: (You will not hear in it any idle talk) [i.e., laghw], and the meaning is that no denial of it will be heard, as said by al-Kisa'i. From this comes the common saying: "'a'idhan billah," meaning "ma'adh Allah" (God forbid), and "qum qa'iman," meaning "qum qiyaman" (stand up). And one of the Arab women, lulling her son, said:

Stand up standing, stand up standing...
You have caught a sleeping slave.

It was also said: "al-kadhibah" is an adjective whose noun is omitted, meaning there is no state of its occurrence that is false, or no soul that is false, i.e., everyone who reports about its occurrence is truthful. Al-Zajjaj said: "(There is no denying its occurrence)" means nothing can repel it. Similar is the saying of al-Hasan and Qatadah. Al-Thawri said: there is no one who denies it. Al-Kisa'i also said: there is no denial of it, i.e., no one should deny it. It was also said: its establishment is a true matter, not a jest.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Bringing low, lifting up﴾. 'Ikrimah, Muqatil and al-Suddi said: it lowers the voice so that it makes those who are near hear, and raises those who are far, meaning it makes the near and the far hear. Al-Suddi said: it brings low the arrogant and raises up the oppressed. Qatadah said: it brings low peoples into the punishment of Allah, and raises up peoples to the obedience of Allah. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it brings low the enemies of Allah into the Fire, and raises up the friends of Allah into Paradise. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: it brings low peoples who were exalted in the world, and raises up peoples who were lowly in the world. Ibn 'Ata' said: it brings low some peoples by justice, and raises up others by grace. "Khafd" (lowering) and "raf'" (raising) are used in Arabic regarding place and rank, and honor and humiliation. Allah, glorified is He, attributed lowering and raising to the Resurrection figuratively and metaphorically, according to the Arabic habit of attributing an act to a place, a time, and other things that are not themselves the agent, as they say: "a sleeping night" and "a fasting day." In the revelation: (Rather, the plotting of the night and the day). The true bringer-low and raiser-up is Allah alone: He raises His friends to the highest ranks and brings low His enemies to the lowest depths. Al-Hasan and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read (khafidatun rafi'atun) in the accusative. The rest read it in the nominative, on the supposition of an omitted subject. Whoever reads it in the accusative does so as a circumstantial accusative (hal). According to al-Farra', it is on the supposition of an omitted verb, and the meaning is: "When the Inevitable Event occurs; there is no denying its occurrence—it occurs bringing low and lifting up." There is no doubt about the occurrence of the Resurrection, and that it raises some peoples and lowers others, as we have explained.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿When the earth is shaken with a shaking﴾, i.e., it is convulsed and moved, according to Mujahid and others. It is said: "rajjahu yarujjuhu rajjan," meaning he moved it and convulsed it. And "naqah rajja'" means one with a large hump. In a hadith: "Whoever boards the sea when it is agitated has no protection," meaning when its waves are turbulent. Al-Kalbi said: that is because when Allah reveals to it, it trembles out of fear of Allah, the Exalted. The exegetes said: it shakes as a child shakes in the cradle, until everything upon it collapses and everything upon it, from mountains and others, is shattered. Ibn 'Abbas said: the rajjah is a violent movement accompanied by a sound. The place of (idha) is in the accusative as a substitute for (idha waqa'at). It is also permissible for it to be governed by (khafidatun rafi'ah), meaning it lowers and raises at the time when the earth is shaken and the mountains are crumbled, because at that time what is high is lowered and what is low is raised. It was also said: the meaning is "The Event occurs when the earth is shaken," as said by al-Zajjaj and al-Jurjani. It was also said: meaning "Remember when the earth is shaken with a shaking," a verbal noun, which is evidence for the repetition of the earthquake.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And the mountains are crumbled to powder﴾, i.e., they are pulverized, according to Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: like flour is crumbled, i.e., kneaded. The "basisah" is toasted flour or meal kneaded with ghee or oil, then eaten without cooking, and it may be taken as provision. The rajiz said:

Do not bake bread and crumbled bread for us,
And do not prolong a halt in a dwelling of constriction.

Abu 'Ubaydah mentioned that he was a thief from Ghatafan who wanted to bake, but feared he would be hurried away from it, so he ate it as dough. The meaning is that they are mixed, becoming like flour kneaded with some water, i.e., the mountains become dust, so some part mixes with another. Al-Hasan said: "bussat" means they were uprooted from their base and went away, akin to His saying: (My Lord will scatter them as scattering). 'Ata'iyyah said: they were spread out like sand and dust. It was also said: "al-bass" means driving, i.e., the mountains are driven. Abu Zayd said: "al-bass" is driving; one says, "I drove the camels, abussuha, bassan." Abu 'Ubayd said: "bassata al-ibil" and "abassta" are two dialects, when you drive them and say to them "bis bis." In a hadith: "A people will go out from Medina to Yemen, Syria and Iraq, driving (yabussuna), and Medina is better for them, if they only knew." And from it another hadith: "The people of Yemen came to you driving their dependents (yabussuna 'iyalahum)." The Arabs say: "Bring it to you from your sensing (hassika) and your driving (bassika)." Abu Zayd transmitted both with a kasrah: "min hassika" means from where you perceived it, and "bassika" means from where your journey reached it. Mujahid said: it flowed as a flood. 'Ikrimah: it was demolished with demolition. Muhammad ibn Ka'b: it was set moving with movement, and from it is the saying of al-Aghlab al-'Ijli [a blank in the manuscripts at the place of the witness from the verse of al-Aghlab al-'Ijli the rajiz, and we have not found it]. Al-Hasan said: it was cut into pieces. The meanings are close.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿So they become scattered dust motes﴾. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "al-hala' al-munbath" is the dust (rahj) that rises from the hooves of animals and then disappears, and Allah made their deeds like that. Mujahid said: "al-habaʾ" is the ray that appears in a window like dust. Something similar is reported from Ibn 'Abbas. Also from him: it is what flies off from fire when it is agitated; sparks fly from it, and when it falls it is nothing. 'Ata'iyyah said likewise. It has passed in (al-Furqan) at His saying: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust motes﴾. The common reading is "munbathhan" with the three-dotted tha', meaning scattered, from His saying: ﴿And He scattered therein every creature﴾, i.e., He dispersed and spread them. Masruq, al-Nakha'i and Abu Haywah read "munbattan" with a two-dotted ta', meaning cut off, from the saying of people: "battahu Allah," i.e., He cut it off, and from it "al-battat."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 56, verses 7–12:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you will be three kinds﴾, meaning three categories, each kind resembling what it belongs to, as a husband resembles his wife. Then He explained who they are, saying: ﴿the companions of the right﴾, ﴿the companions of the left﴾, and ﴿the foremost﴾. The companions of the right are those who are taken by way of the right (dhat al-yamin) to Paradise, and the companions of the left (mash'ama) are those who are taken by way of the left (dhat al-shimal) to the Fire. This was said by al-Suddi. Al-Mash'ama is the left side, and likewise al-Sha'ama. It is said: "So-and-so sat on the left (sha'ama)." It is also said: "O so-and-so, take your companions to the left (shā'im bi-aṣḥābika)," meaning take them to the left side. The Arabs call the left hand al-shu'ma, and the left side al-ash'am. Likewise, what comes from the right is called al-yumn, and what comes from the left is called al-shu'm.

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi said: The companions of the right are those who were on the right of Adam when the offspring were brought forth from his loins, and Allah said to them: "These are for Paradise, and I do not mind." Zayd ibn Aslam said: The companions of the right are those who were taken from the right side of Adam on that day, and the companions of the left are those who were taken from his left side. 'Ata' and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: The companions of the right are whoever is given his book in his right hand, and the companions of the left are whoever is given his book in his left hand. Ibn Jurayj said: The companions of the right are the people of good deeds, and the companions of the left are the people of evil deeds. Al-Hasan and al-Rabi' said: The companions of the right are those blessed for their own souls through righteous deeds, and the companions of the left are those cursed for their own souls through evil and ugly deeds.

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of the Night Journey (isra'), from Abu Dharr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "When we ascended to the lowest heaven, there was a man, with black shapes (aswida) on his right and black shapes on his left. When he looked to his right he laughed, and when he looked to his left he wept. He said: 'Welcome, O righteous prophet and righteous son!' I said: 'O Jibril, who is this?' He said: 'This is Adam, peace be upon him, and these shapes on his right and on his left are the souls (nasam) of his descendants. The people of the right are the people of Paradise, and the shapes on his left are the people of the Fire.'" And he mentioned the hadith.

Al-Mubarrad said: The companions of the right are the companions of precedence (al-taqaddum), and the companions of the left are the companions of delay (al-ta'akhkhur). The Arabs say: "Place me on your right and do not place me on your left," meaning: make me among those who go ahead, and do not make us among those who fall behind.

The repetition in ﴿What are the companions of the right?﴾ and ﴿What are the companions of the left?﴾ is for magnification and wonder, like His saying: ﴿The Inevitable Reality, what is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ and ﴿The Striking Calamity, what is the Striking Calamity?﴾, just as one says: "Zayd, what Zayd is!" In the hadith of Umm Zar', may Allah be pleased with her: "Malik, and what Malik is!"[[The hadith of Umm Zar' is narrated by Muslim in the Book of the Virtues of the Companions, from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that eleven women sat together, made a pact and agreed not to conceal any news of their husbands. One of them said: "My husband is Malik, and what Malik is! Malik is better than that..." etc. [The hadith].]] The intended meaning is to magnify the reward of the companions of the right and the punishment of the companions of the left.

It has been said: ﴿the companions﴾ (fa-aṣḥābu) is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject), and the predicate (khabar, the grammatical predicate) is ﴿What are the companions of the right?﴾, as if he said: "The companions of the right, what are they? What are they?" The meaning is: what kind of people they are. It has also been said that ﴿mā﴾ may be for emphasis, and the meaning is: those who are given their book in their right hands are the people of precedence and high rank.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The foremost are those who, when the truth is given to them, accept it, and when they are asked for it, they give it, and they judge people as they judge themselves." This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: They are the prophets. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: They are the foremost to faith from every nation. Similar was said by 'Ikrimah. Muhammad ibn Sirin said: They are those who prayed towards both qiblas (the two directions of prayer). The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers﴾.[[See vol. 8, p. 235.]] Mujahid and others said: They are the foremost to jihad, and the first people to go to prayer early. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: They are the foremost to the five prayers. al-Dahhak said: They are the foremost to jihad. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: They are the foremost to repentance and acts of righteousness. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord﴾,[[See vol. 4, p. 203.]] then He praised them, saying: ﴿Those hasten to good deeds, and they are foremost in them﴾.[[See vol. 12, p. 133.]]

It was said that they are four: among them is the foremost of the nation of Musa, who is Hizqil, the believer of the family of Pharaoh; and the foremost of the nation of 'Isa, who is Habib al-Najjar, the companion of Antakya; and two foremost in the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ), who are Abu Bakr and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and related by al-Mawardi. Shumayt ibn al-'Ajlan said: People are of three kinds. A man who got an early start on goodness in the freshness of his youth and persisted in it until he left this world; this is the foremost, the one brought near. A man who began his life with sins, then long heedlessness, then returned in repentance until it was sealed for him; this is among the companions of the right. And a man who began his life with sins and never ceased in them until it was sealed for him in them; this is among the companions of the left. It was also said: They are everyone who precedes others in any of the things of righteousness.

Then it was said: ﴿the foremost﴾ is in the nominative as the subject, the second is an emphasis for it, and the predicate is ﴿those are the ones brought near﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿the foremost﴾ is in the nominative as the subject, and the second is its predicate. The meaning is: the foremost to the obedience of Allah are the foremost to the mercy of Allah; ﴿those are the ones brought near﴾ is a description of them. It was also said: When a man from the foremost, the brought-near, leaves his dwelling in Paradise, he has a light by which he is recognized by those beneath him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 56, verses 17–26:

The words of God Most High: ﴿Youths who remain ever young will circulate among them﴾, meaning boys who do not die. This is the view of Mujahid. Al-Hasan and al-Kalbi said: they do not age and they do not change. From this is the line of Imru' al-Qays:

*"Will they enjoy anything but a happy one who is ever young, / with few worries, who does not spend the night in fear?"*

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Mukhalladun" means "wearing earrings." The earring is called *al-khalda*, and the collection of ornaments is called *al-khildah*. It was also said: "adorned with bracelets," and this was reported from al-Farra'. The poet said:

*"And ever-young ones adorned with silver, as if their buttocks / were sand dunes."*

[The word *al-aqawiz* is the plural of *qawz*, a small sand dune. The buttocks of women are compared to it, so the construction is a genitive of explanation (*idafat al-bayan*).]

It was also said: "adorned with earrings" means "girdled with belts" (*mumanTaqun*). Ikrimah said: "mukhalladun" means "made luxurious." It was also said: they are of one age, whom God created for the people of Paradise to circulate among them as He wills, without birth. Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, and al-Hasan al-Basri said: the *wildan* here are the children of the Muslims who die young, with neither good deeds nor bad deeds. Salman al-Farisi said: the children of the polytheists will be the servants of the people of Paradise. Al-Hasan said: they had no good deeds for which they would be rewarded, nor bad deeds for which they would be punished, so they were placed in this position. The purpose is that the people of Paradise are in the utmost joy and blessing, and blessing is only complete when servants and youths surround a person.

﴿with cups and jugs﴾. *Akwab* is the plural of *kub*, which was discussed in surah al-Zukhruf [see vol. 16, p. 112]. It is a vessel without a handle or spout. *Abariq* are vessels with handles and spouts; the singular is *ibriq*, named so because its color gleams (*yabriqu*) from its clarity.

﴿and a cup from a flowing spring﴾. This was discussed in surah al-Saffat [see vol. 15, p. 77]. *Ma'in* means flowing, whether of water or wine. In this context, however, it means wine flowing from springs. It was also said: "visible to the springs," so that *ma'in* would be a passive participle from *mu'aynah* (seeing). It was also said: it is *fa'il* from *al-ma'n*, which means abundance. He explained that it is not like the wine of this world, which is extracted by pressing, effort and processing.

The words of God Most High: ﴿They will not be made faint by it﴾, meaning their heads will not split from drinking it. That is, its delight is without harm, unlike the drinks of this world.

﴿Nor will they be intoxicated﴾. This was discussed in surah al-Saffat, meaning they will not become drunk so that their minds are lost. Mujahid recited *la yusaddaAna* (with the verb read as "they will not be split apart"), meaning "they will not scatter," as in His words: ﴿on that day they will be separated﴾ [see vol. 14, p. 42]. The people of Kufa read *yunzifun* with a kasra on the *zay*, meaning their drink will not run out and their wine will not be exhausted. From this is the line of the poet [this is al-Hutay'a, and the verse was cited previously in vol. 15, p. 79]:

*"By my life, if you were exhausted or sober, / you would be the worst companions, the family of Abjar."*

Al-Dahhak reported from Ibn Abbas that he said: wine has four properties: intoxication, headache, vomiting and urination. God mentioned the wine of Paradise and exempted it from these properties.

The words of God Most High: ﴿and fruit of whatever they choose﴾, meaning they choose whatever they wish because of its abundance. It was also said: fruit that is chosen and pleasing. *Takhayyur* means choosing.

﴿and the flesh of birds of whatever they desire﴾. Al-Tirmidhi reported from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked, "What is al-Kawthar?" He said: "That is a river God gave me, meaning in Paradise, whiter than milk and sweeter than honey, in which are birds whose necks are like the necks of camels." Umar said: "Indeed these are luxurious." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever eats them is better than them." [In the manuscripts of the original: "whoever eats them is more luxurious than them." What we have written is in Sahih al-Tirmidhi.] He said: it is a good hadith. Al-Tha'labi transmitted from the hadith of Abu al-Darda' that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "In Paradise there are birds like the necks of Bactrian camels, which line up at the hand of a friend of God. One of them says, 'O friend of God, I grazed in meadows beneath the Throne and drank from the springs of Tasnim, so eat from me.' They continue to boast before him until the thought of eating one of them crosses his heart, and then they fall before him in various colors. He eats from them whatever he wishes. When he is satisfied, the bones of the bird gather together and it flies off to graze in Paradise wherever it wishes." Umar said: "O Prophet of God, they are indeed luxurious for us." He said: "Its eater is more luxurious than it." It was also reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "In Paradise there is a bird within the bird, of which there are seventy thousand feathers. It lands on the dish of a man of the people of Paradise, then shakes itself, and from every feather comes a food, whiter than snow, colder, softer than butter and sweeter than honey, with no color resembling its companion. He eats from it what he wishes, then it departs and flies off."

The words of God Most High: ﴿and wide-eyed maidens [ḥūr ʿīn]﴾. This was recited with *raf'* (nominative), *nasb* (accusative) and *jarr* (genitive). Whoever read it in the genitive, which was Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and others, it may be coordinated with *bi-akwab* (with cups). This is understood by meaning, because the sense is "they enjoy cups, fruit, flesh and wide-eyed maidens," as al-Zajjaj said. It may also be coordinated with *jannat* (gardens), meaning they are in *jannat al-na'im* (gardens of bliss), and in the wide-eyed maidens, with an ellipsis of the genitive construction, as if he said: "and in the company of wide-eyed maidens." Al-Farra' said: the genitive is by agreement in form, even though the meanings differ, because the maidens are not circulated. The poet said:

*"When the coquettes appear one day, / and they arch their eyebrows and eyes."*

But the eye is not arched; it is painted with kohl. Another said:

*"I saw your husband in battle, / girding a sword and a spear."*

Qutrub said: it is coordinated with *al-akwab* and *al-abariq* without understanding it by meaning. He said: it is not denied that they may circulate among them with the maidens, and there may be pleasure for them in that. Whoever read it in the accusative, which was al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli, al-Nakha'i, 'Isa ibn 'Umar al-Thaqafi, and so it is in the codex of Ubayy, then it is by supposing a hidden verb, as if he said: "and they will be married to wide-eyed maidens." Understanding it in the accusative by meaning is also good, because the meaning of "they are circulated with it" is "they are given it." Whoever read it in the nominative, which is the majority, and was the choice of Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim, then it is by the meaning "and with them are wide-eyed maidens," because the maidens are not circulated among them. Al-Kisa'i said: whoever read *wa-hurun 'inun* in the nominative and gave as reason that they are not circulated, must apply the same to fruit and flesh, because these are not circulated; only wine is circulated. Al-Akhfash said: it may be understood by meaning, because the meaning is "they have cups, and they have wide-eyed maidens." It may also be coordinated with *thullah* (a group), and *thullah* is the subject, with its predicate being *'ala sururin mawdunah* (upon woven couches). Likewise "and wide-eyed maidens." He began with an indefinite noun because it is specified by its description.

﴿like hidden pearls﴾, meaning like the likeness of hidden pearls, which are the ones no hands have touched and no dust has settled upon. They are thus at the utmost purity and luster. That is, in the harmony of their bodies they are beautiful from all sides, as the poet said:

*"As if she were created within the shell of a pearl, / every side of her is a face for the watchers."*

﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾, meaning a recompense, and it is in the accusative as an object of purpose. It may also be an absolute object, because the meaning of ﴿youths who remain ever young will circulate among them﴾ is "they will be recompensed." The discussion of the wide-eyed maidens has already passed in surah al-Tur [see p. 65 of this part and vol. 16, p. 152] and elsewhere. Anas said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God created the wide-eyed maidens from saffron." Khalid ibn al-Walid said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "Indeed a man of the people of Paradise holds an apple from the apples of Paradise, and it splits in his hand, and from it comes out a maiden [ḥawrā'] who, if she looked at the sun, would shame the sun with her beauty, without the apple being diminished." A man said to him: "O Abu Sulayman, this is strange. Is the apple not diminished?" He said: "Yes, like a lamp lit from which another lamp is lit, and the lamp is not diminished. God is capable of whatever He wills." It was reported from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he said: God created the wide-eyed maidens from the toes of their feet up to their knees from saffron, from their knees to their breasts from pure musk, from their breasts to their necks from grey ambergris, from their necks to their heads from white camphor. Upon her are seventy thousand robes like the anemones [shaqa'iq al-Nu'man: a plant with red flowers; the singular is *shaqiqat al-Nu'man*]. When she approaches, her face shines with bright light, as the sun shines for the people of the world. When she turns away, her liver can be seen through the thinness of her garments and skin. On her head are seventy thousand locks of pure musk, and for each lock there is a servant girl who lifts her train while calling out: "This is the reward of the friends of God," ﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾.

Al-Hasan said: they had no good deeds for which they would be rewarded, nor bad deeds for which they would be punished, so they were placed in this position. The purpose is that the people of Paradise are in the utmost joy and blessing, and blessing is only complete when servants and youths surround a person.

﴿with cups and jugs﴾. *Akwab* is the plural of *kub*, which was discussed in surah al-Zukhruf [see vol. 16, p. 112]. It is a vessel without a handle or spout. *Abariq* are vessels with handles and spouts; the singular is *ibriq*, named so because its color gleams (*yabriqu*) from its clarity.

﴿and a cup from a flowing spring﴾. This was discussed in surah al-Saffat [see vol. 15, p. 77]. *Ma'in* means flowing, whether of water or wine. In this context, however, it means wine flowing from springs. It was also said: "visible to the springs," so that *ma'in* would be a passive participle from *mu'aynah* (seeing). It was also said: it is *fa'il* from *al-ma'n*, which means abundance. He explained that it is not like the wine of this world, which is extracted by pressing, effort and processing.

The words of God Most High: ﴿They will not be made faint by it﴾, meaning their heads will not split from drinking it. That is, its delight is without harm, unlike the drinks of this world.

﴿Nor will they be intoxicated﴾. This was discussed in surah al-Saffat, meaning they will not become drunk so that their minds are lost. Mujahid recited *la yusaddaAna* (with the verb read as "they will not be split apart"), meaning "they will not scatter," as in His words: ﴿on that day they will be separated﴾ [see vol. 14, p. 42]. The people of Kufa read *yunzifun* with a kasra on the *zay*, meaning their drink will not run out and their wine will not be exhausted. From this is the line of the poet [this is al-Hutay'a, and the verse was cited previously in vol. 15, p. 79]:

*"By my life, if you were exhausted or sober, / you would be the worst companions, the family of Abjar."*

Al-Dahhak reported from Ibn Abbas that he said: wine has four properties: intoxication, headache, vomiting and urination. God mentioned the wine of Paradise and exempted it from these properties.

The words of God Most High: ﴿and fruit of whatever they choose﴾, meaning they choose whatever they wish because of its abundance. It was also said: fruit that is chosen and pleasing. *Takhayyur* means choosing.

﴿and the flesh of birds of whatever they desire﴾. Al-Tirmidhi reported from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked, "What is al-Kawthar?" He said: "That is a river God gave me, meaning in Paradise, whiter than milk and sweeter than honey, in which are birds whose necks are like the necks of camels." Umar said: "Indeed these are luxurious." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever eats them is better than them." [In the manuscripts of the original: "whoever eats them is more luxurious than them." What we have written is in Sahih al-Tirmidhi.] He said: it is a good hadith. Al-Tha'labi transmitted from the hadith of Abu al-Darda' that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "In Paradise there are birds like the necks of Bactrian camels, which line up at the hand of a friend of God. One of them says, 'O friend of God, I grazed in meadows beneath the Throne and drank from the springs of Tasnim, so eat from me.' They continue to boast before him until the thought of eating one of them crosses his heart, and then they fall before him in various colors. He eats from them whatever he wishes. When he is satisfied, the bones of the bird gather together and it flies off to graze in Paradise wherever it wishes." Umar said: "O Prophet of God, they are indeed luxurious for us." He said: "Its eater is more luxurious than it." It was also reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "In Paradise there is a bird within the bird, of which there are seventy thousand feathers. It lands on the dish of a man of the people of Paradise, then shakes itself, and from every feather comes a food, whiter than snow, colder, softer than butter and sweeter than honey, with no color resembling its companion. He eats from it what he wishes, then it departs and flies off."

The words of God Most High: ﴿and wide-eyed maidens [ḥūr ʿīn]﴾. This was recited with *raf'* (nominative), *nasb* (accusative) and *jarr* (genitive). Whoever read it in the genitive, which was Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and others, it may be coordinated with *bi-akwab* (with cups). This is understood by meaning, because the sense is "they enjoy cups, fruit, flesh and wide-eyed maidens," as al-Zajjaj said. It may also be coordinated with *jannat* (gardens), meaning they are in *jannat al-na'im* (gardens of bliss), and in the wide-eyed maidens, with an ellipsis of the genitive construction, as if he said: "and in the company of wide-eyed maidens." Al-Farra' said: the genitive is by agreement in form, even though the meanings differ, because the maidens are not circulated. The poet said:

*"When the coquettes appear one day, / and they arch their eyebrows and eyes."*

But the eye is not arched; it is painted with kohl. Another said:

*"I saw your husband in battle, / girding a sword and a spear."*

Qutrub said: it is coordinated with *al-akwab* and *al-abariq* without understanding it by meaning. He said: it is not denied that they may circulate among them with the maidens, and there may be pleasure for them in that. Whoever read it in the accusative, which was al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli, al-Nakha'i, 'Isa ibn 'Umar al-Thaqafi, and so it is in the codex of Ubayy, then it is by supposing a hidden verb, as if he said: "and they will be married to wide-eyed maidens." Understanding it in the accusative by meaning is also good, because the meaning of "they are circulated with it" is "they are given it." Whoever read it in the nominative, which is the majority, and was the choice of Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim, then it is by the meaning "and with them are wide-eyed maidens," because the maidens are not circulated among them. Al-Kisa'i said: whoever read *wa-hurun 'inun* in the nominative and gave as reason that they are not circulated, must apply the same to fruit and flesh, because these are not circulated; only wine is circulated. Al-Akhfash said: it may be understood by meaning, because the meaning is "they have cups, and they have wide-eyed maidens." It may also be coordinated with *thullah* (a group), and *thullah* is the subject, with its predicate being *'ala sururin mawdunah* (upon woven couches). Likewise "and wide-eyed maidens." He began with an indefinite noun because it is specified by its description.

﴿like hidden pearls﴾, meaning like the likeness of hidden pearls, which are the ones no hands have touched and no dust has settled upon. They are thus at the utmost purity and luster. That is, in the harmony of their bodies they are beautiful from all sides, as the poet said:

*"As if she were created within the shell of a pearl, / every side of her is a face for the watchers."*

﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾, meaning a recompense, and it is in the accusative as an object of purpose. It may also be an absolute object, because the meaning of ﴿youths who remain ever young will circulate among them﴾ is "they will be recompensed." The discussion of the wide-eyed maidens has already passed in surah al-Tur [see p. 65 of this part and vol. 16, p. 152] and elsewhere. Anas said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God created the wide-eyed maidens from saffron." Khalid ibn al-Walid said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "Indeed a man of the people of Paradise holds an apple from the apples of Paradise, and it splits in his hand, and from it comes out a maiden [ḥawrā'] who, if she looked at the sun, would shame the sun with her beauty, without the apple being diminished." A man said to him: "O Abu Sulayman, this is strange. Is the apple not diminished?" He said: "Yes, like a lamp lit from which another lamp is lit, and the lamp is not diminished. God is capable of whatever He wills." It was reported from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he said: God created the wide-eyed maidens from the toes of their feet up to their knees from saffron, from their knees to their breasts from pure musk, from their breasts to their necks from grey ambergris, from their necks to their heads from white camphor. Upon her are seventy thousand robes like the anemones [shaqa'iq al-Nu'man: a plant with red flowers; the singular is *shaqiqat al-Nu'man*]. When she approaches, her face shines with bright light, as the sun shines for the people of the world. When she turns away, her liver can be seen through the thinness of her garments and skin. On her head are seventy thousand locks of pure musk, and for each lock there is a servant girl who lifts her train while calling out: "This is the reward of the friends of God," ﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾.

The words of God Most High: ﴿They will not hear therein any vain talk or sinful speech﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "vain" means falsehood and lies. *Laghw* is what is discarded from speech, and *ta'thim* is a verbal noun from *atham-tuhu*, meaning "I told him, you have sinned." Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: ﴿nor sinful speech﴾ means that none of them charges another with sin. Mujahid said: ﴿They will not hear therein vain talk or sinful speech﴾ means cursing or sin.

﴿except the word "Peace, peace"﴾. *Qilan* is in the accusative governed by *yasma'una* (they hear), or it is an exceptional construction that is disconnected, meaning "but they say a word" or "they hear." *Salaman salaman* are in the accusative governed by "saying," meaning "except that they say good things." Or it is in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning "except that one of them says to another, 'Salam.'" Or it is an adjective of *qilan*, and the second *salam* is a substitute for the first, and the meaning is "except a speech in which one is safe from vain talk." It is permissible to read it in the nominative, by supposing "Peace be upon you." Ibn Abbas said: meaning that some of them greet others. It was also said: the angels greet them, or their Lord, Mighty and Majestic, greets them.

*"Will they enjoy anything but a happy one who is ever young, / with few worries, who does not spend the night in fear?"*

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Mukhalladun" means "wearing earrings." The earring is called *al-khalda*, and the collection of ornaments is called *al-khildah*. It was also said: "adorned with bracelets," and this was reported from al-Farra'. The poet said:

*"And ever-young ones adorned with silver, as if their buttocks / were sand dunes."*

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 56, verses 27–40 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And the companions of the right hand: what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ This returns to the mention of the ranks of the companions of the right hand, who are the foremost, as has preceded. The repetition is to magnify the greatness of the bounty in which they dwell.

(﴿Among lote-trees with thorns removed﴾): that is, among lote-trees (nabq) whose thorns have been removed, meaning cut off. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others. Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned: Safwan related to us from Sulaym ibn 'Amir, who said: The Companions of the Prophet ﷺ used to say: "Indeed the bedouin Arabs and their questions benefit us." He said: One day a bedouin came and said: "O Messenger of Allah! Allah has mentioned in the Qur'an a tree that causes harm, and I did not think there was in Paradise a tree that harms its owner." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "And what is it?" He said: "The lote-tree (sidr), for it has harmful thorns." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Does He not say: ﴿among lote-trees with thorns removed﴾? Allah has removed its thorns and has made in place of every thorn a fruit, and it brings forth fruit which splits open to reveal seventy-two kinds of food, no two of which resemble each other." Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Dahhak said: The Muslims looked at Wajj (and it is [[What is in al-Lisan: Wajj is a place in the desert. It was also said: a town in al-Ta'if, and it was also said it is al-Ta'if.]] a valley in al-Ta'if that is fertile), and they admired its lote-trees, and they said: "Would that we had the like of this!" So this was revealed. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt, describing Paradise, said:

"Indeed the gardens in the Gardens are shaded, / among them the full-breasted maidens, and their lote-trees are thornless."

Al-Dahhak, Mujahid and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: ﴿among lote-trees with thorns removed﴾ means laden with fruit. This is close to what we have mentioned in the report. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: its fruit is larger than the large jars. This has already passed in Surah al-Najm at His saying: ﴿at the lote-tree of the utmost boundary﴾, and that its fruit is like the jars of Hajar, from the hadith of Anas from the Prophet ﷺ. [[See p. 94 and p. 5 of this part.]]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And acacia trees arranged in tiers﴾. Talh is the banana tree, its singular being talhah. This was said by most of the exegetes: 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and others. Al-Hasan said: it is not the banana, but a tree that has cool, moist shade. Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubaydah said: large trees that have thorns. One of the reciters [[So in the originals, (al-Hudat) with the unpointed ha'. In Tafsir al-Tabari it is (al-Judat) with the jim.]] said, and he is al-Ja'di:

"Her guide gave her good news and they said: / Tomorrow you will see the acacia and the ahbal [[al-Ahbal is the plural of habalah, with a damma: the fruit of the salam and bal and samur trees, or the fruit of the 'idah trees in general.]]."

So talh is every large tree with abundant thorns. Al-Zajjaj said: it is possible that it is in Paradise but its thorns have been removed. Al-Zajjaj also said: like the tree of Umm Ghaylan [it has [[An addition required by the context.]]] a very fragrant blossom; so they were addressed and promised what they love like it, except that its excellence over what is in this world is like the excellence of all that is in Paradise over what is in this world. Al-Suddi said: the acacia of Paradise resembles the acacia of this world, but it has fruit sweeter than honey. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, recited: ﴿and banana [ṭalʿ] arranged in tiers﴾ with the 'ayn, and he recited this verse: ﴿and palm trees whose spathes are fine-clustered﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 127.]]. This is contrary to the Mushaf. In a report it is said that he was recited before him: ﴿and acacia trees arranged in tiers﴾, and he said: "What is wrong with the acacia? It is only ﴿and banana arranged in tiers﴾." Then he said: ﴿it has spathes stacked in layers﴾. It was said to him: "Shall we not change it?" He said: "The Qur'an should not be stirred up and changed." So he preferred this reading but did not regard it as being written in the Mushaf, because it contradicts what its script has agreed upon. This was said by al-Qushayri. Abu Bakr al-Anbari supported it with a chain, saying: My father related to me, saying: al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah related to us, saying: 'Isa ibn Yunus related to us from Mujalid from al-Hasan ibn Sa'd from Qays ibn 'Abbad, who said: I recited before 'Ali, or it was recited before 'Ali—Mujalid was uncertain—﴿and acacia arranged in tiers﴾, and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "What is the matter with the acacia? Do you not recite ﴿and acacia﴾?" Then he said: ﴿it has spathes stacked in layers﴾. The man said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful, shall we erase it from the Mushaf?" He said: [No, [[An addition from B.]] the Qur'an is not to be stirred up today.] Abu Bakr said: The meaning of this is that he returned to what is in the Mushaf and knew that it was the correct reading, and he nullified what had come from his earlier statement. Al-manḍūd is the one that is layered upon itself, which has been arranged [[An addition from B.]] at its beginning and its end with its fruit; it has no visible stems, but is tightly packed. Al-nadd is the packing, and al-munaḍḍad is that which is packed tightly. Al-Nabighah said:

"She left the path of a donkey which was holding him back / and raised him to the two curtains and the arranged [piles]."

Masruq said: The trees of Paradise, from their roots to their branches, are arranged in tiers, all fruit. Whenever one eats a fruit, another grows in its place, better than it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and extended shade﴾, that is, lasting and enduring, which does not cease and is not removed by the sun, as in His saying: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord extends the shade? And had He willed, He would have made it stationary﴾. This is in the morning, which is the period between the first light of dawn and the rising of the sun, as its explanation has already preceded there [[See vol. 13, p. 37.]]. The repetition is to magnify the greatness of the bounty in which they dwell.

Allah has removed its thorns and has made in place of every thorn a fruit, and it brings forth fruit which splits open to reveal seventy-two kinds of food, no two of which resemble each other." Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Dahhak said: The Muslims looked at Wajj (and it is [[What is in al-Lisan: Wajj is a place in the desert. It was also said: a town in al-Ta'if, and it was also said it is al-Ta'if.]] a valley in al-Ta'if that is fertile), and they admired its lote-trees, and they said: "Would that we had the like of this!" "Indeed the gardens in the Gardens are shaded, / among them the full-breasted maidens, and their lote-trees are thornless."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: its fruit is larger than the large jars. This has already passed in Surah al-Najm at His saying: ﴿at the lote-tree of the utmost boundary﴾, and that its fruit is like the jars of Hajar, from the hadith of Anas from the Prophet ﷺ. [[See p. 94 and p. 5 of this part.]]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And acacia trees arranged in tiers﴾. Talh is the banana tree, its singular being talhah. This was said by most of the exegetes: 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and others. Al-Hasan said: it is not the banana, but a tree that has cool, moist shade. Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubaydah said: large trees that have thorns. One of the reciters [[So in the originals, (al-Hudat) with the unpointed ha'. In Tafsir al-Tabari it is (al-Judat) with the jim.]] said, and he is al-Ja'di:

"Her guide gave her good news and they said: / Tomorrow you will see the acacia and the ahbal [[al-Ahbal is the plural of habalah, with a damma: the fruit of the salam and bal and samur trees, or the fruit of the 'idah trees in general.]]."

So talh is every large tree with abundant thorns. Al-Zajjaj said: it is possible that it is in Paradise but its thorns have been removed. Al-Zajjaj also said: like the tree of Umm Ghaylan [it has [[An addition required by the context.]]] a very fragrant blossom; so they were addressed and promised what they love like it, except that its excellence over what is in this world is like the excellence of all that is in Paradise over what is in this world. Al-Suddi said: the acacia of Paradise resembles the acacia of this world, but it has fruit sweeter than honey. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, recited: ﴿and banana [ṭalʿ] arranged in tiers﴾ with the 'ayn, and he recited this verse: ﴿and palm trees whose spathes are fine-clustered﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 127.]]. This is contrary to the Mushaf. In a report it is said that he was recited before him: ﴿and acacia trees arranged in tiers﴾, and he said: "What is wrong with the acacia? It is only ﴿and banana arranged in tiers﴾." Then he said: ﴿it has spathes stacked in layers﴾. It was said to him: "Shall we not change it?" He said: "The Qur'an should not be stirred up and changed." So he preferred this reading but did not regard it as being written in the Mushaf, because it contradicts what its script has agreed upon. This was said by al-Qushayri. Abu Bakr al-Anbari supported it with a chain, saying: My father related to me, saying: al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah related to us, saying: 'Isa ibn Yunus related to us from Mujalid from al-Hasan ibn Sa'd from Qays ibn 'Abbad, who said: I recited before 'Ali, or it was recited before 'Ali—Mujalid was uncertain—﴿and acacia arranged in tiers﴾, and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "What is the matter with the acacia? Do you not recite ﴿and acacia﴾?" Then he said: ﴿it has spathes stacked in layers﴾. The man said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful, shall we erase it from the Mushaf?" He said: [No, [[An addition from B.]] the Qur'an is not to be stirred up today.] Abu Bakr said: The meaning of this is that he returned to what is in the Mushaf and knew that it was the correct reading, and he nullified what had come from his earlier statement. Al-manḍūd is the one that is layered upon itself, which has been arranged [[An addition from B.]] at its beginning and its end with its fruit; it has no visible stems, but is tightly packed. Al-nadd is the packing, and al-munaḍḍad is that which is packed tightly. Al-Nabighah said:

"She left the path of a donkey which was holding him back / and raised him to the two curtains and the arranged [piles]."

Masruq said: The trees of Paradise, from their roots to their branches, are arranged in tiers, all fruit. Whenever one eats a fruit, another grows in its place, better than it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and extended shade﴾, that is, lasting and enduring, which does not cease and is not removed by the sun, as in His saying: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord extends the shade? And had He willed, He would have made it stationary﴾. This is in the morning, which is the period between the first light of dawn and the rising of the sun, as its explanation has already preceded there [[See vol. 13, p. 37.]]. The whole of Paradise is shade with no sun in it. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: it means the shade of the Throne. 'Amr ibn Maymun said: a distance of seventy thousand years. Abu 'Ubaydah said: The Arabs say of a long age, a long life, and a thing that does not end, that it is "extended" (mamdud). Labid said:

"Endurance has prevailed, and I was not one to be overcome: / a long age, lasting and extended."

In the Sahih of al-Tirmidhi and others, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet ﷺ: "In Paradise there is a tree in whose shade a rider could travel for a hundred years without crossing it. Recite, if you wish: ﴿and extended shade﴾."

﴿And flowing water﴾, that is, running and never ceasing. The root of sakb is pouring; it is said: sakaba sakban, and al-sukub is its pouring out, and it is said: sakaba sukuban, and insakaba insikaban, meaning poured water flowing night and day in a channel without interruption, never cut off from them. The Arabs were people of the desert and hot lands, and rivers were rare in their countries; they could not reach water except with a bucket and rope. So they were promised in Paradise the opposite of that, and were described the familiar sources of delight of this world: trees and their shade, and waters and rivers flowing in succession.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and abundant fruit﴾, that is, not scarce and rare as it was in their countries; ﴿not cut off﴾, that is, at any time, as the fruits of summer are cut off in winter; ﴿nor forbidden﴾, that is, not restricted against them as the fruits of this world are. It was also said: ﴿nor forbidden﴾ means no one who desires them is prevented by thorns or distance or a wall; rather, when the servant desires it, it draws near to him until he takes it. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and its clusters are made near, [bowing low]﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 137.]]. It was also said: they are not cut off by seasons, nor forbidden by prices. And Allah knows best.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and raised couches﴾. al-Tirmidhi related from Abu Sa'id from the Prophet ﷺ concerning His saying: ﴿and raised couches﴾: he said: "Their height is for you both between heaven and earth, a distance of five hundred years." He said: This is a strange hadith which we do not know except from the hadith of Rishdin ibn Sa'd. Some scholars said in explaining this hadith: the couches are in the ranks, and the distance between the ranks is like the distance between heaven and earth. It was also said: the couches here are a metaphor for the women of Paradise who have not been previously mentioned; but the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and raised couches﴾ indicate them, because they are the place of women. So the meaning is: and women high in rank in their beauty and perfection. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿Indeed We have produced them with a [special] production﴾, that is, We created them in a creation and originated them in an origination. The Arabs call a woman a "bed," a "garment," and a "wrapper," and Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿They are clothing for you﴾ [[See vol. 2, p. 316.]]. Then it was said: according to this, they are the wide-eyed maidens (hur 'in), that is, We created them without birth. It was also said: the meaning is the women of the children of Adam, that is, We created them with a new creation, which is restoration: We restored them to the state of youth and perfect beauty. The meaning is that We produced the old woman and the young girl in a single production. They are described as pronouns without prior mention, because they have entered among the companions of the right hand, and because the couches are a metaphor for women, as has preceded. It has been related from the Prophet ﷺ concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed We have produced them with a [special] production﴾ that he said: "Among them are virgins and non-virgins." Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: I asked the Prophet ﷺ about His saying: ﴿Indeed We have produced them with a [special] production, and made them virgins, loving, of equal age﴾, and he said: "O Umm Salamah, they are those who died in this world as old women, toothless, with weak eyes and watery eyes; Allah made them, after old age, of equal age, of one birth in uniformity." Al-Nahhas supported it with a chain from Anas, who said: Ahmad ibn 'Amr related to us, saying: 'Amr ibn 'Ali related to us, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us from Musa ibn 'Ubaydah, from Yazid al-Raqashi, from Anas ibn Malik, who raised it: ﴿Indeed We have produced them with a [special] production﴾, he said: "They are the old women, toothless and with watery eyes, who were in this world toothless with watery eyes." Al-Musayyib ibn Sharik said: The Prophet ﷺ said concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed We have produced them with a [special] production﴾ [the verse [[An addition from B.]]], he said: "They are the old women of this world. Allah produces them with a new creation, so that whenever their husbands come to them they find them virgins." When 'A'ishah heard that she said: "Oh, my pain!" So the Prophet ﷺ said to her: "There is no pain there."

(﴿'uruban﴾) is the plural of 'arub. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others said: al-'urub are women who are passionate toward their husbands. Also from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the ʿarūb, the coquettish. 'Ikrimah: the flirtatious. Ibn Zayd: in the dialect of the people of Madinah. From this is the saying of Labid:

"And in the howdah is an 'arub, not indecent, / with buttocks that are full, before whom the eye is dazzled."

It is the shaklah in the dialect of the people of Makkah. Also from Zayd ibn Aslam: the one good in speech. Also from 'Ikrimah and Qatadah: the 'urub are those who show affection to their husbands, and its derivation is from a'rab, meaning to make clear; so the 'arub makes her love for her husband clear by coquetry, flirtation and good speech. It was said: she is the one who is good in obedience (tab'ul), that is, submissive to her husband out of love for him, so that she may be more pleasurable to enjoy. Ja'far ibn Muhammad related from his father from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said concerning ('uruban): "Their speech is Arabic." Hamzah and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited ('urban) with a sukun on the ra'. The rest recited it with a damma, and both are permissible in the plural of fa'ul.

(﴿atraban﴾): of one birth in uniformity and one age of thirty-three years. It is said of women atrab, and of men aqran. The Arabs used to incline toward women who had passed the limit of youth but had not reached old age. It was also said: atraban means equals and similar ones; this was said by Mujahid. Al-Suddi: atrab in character, with no hatred or envy among them. It was said: the wide-eyed maidens are for the foremost, and the atrab, the 'urub, are for the companions of the right hand.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿A company of the earlier generations, and a company of the later ones.﴾ The discourse returns to His words: (And the companions of the right hand — what are the companions of the right hand?) That is, they are (a company of the earlier generations, and a company of the later ones), and the meaning of this has already been discussed.

Abu al-Aliyah, Mujahid, Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and al-Dahhak said: (A company of the earlier generations) means the early ones of this Ummah (and a company of the later ones) means the later ones of this Ummah. What supports this is what was narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding this verse, (A company of the earlier generations, and a company of the later ones), that the Prophet ﷺ said: "They are all from my Ummah."

Al-Wahidi said: the companions of the Garden are of two halves: a half from the past nations and a half from this Ummah. This is refuted by what Ibn Majah related in his Sunan and al-Tirmidhi in his Jami' from Buraydah ibn Khusayb (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The people of Paradise are one hundred and twenty rows; eighty of them are from this Ummah and forty from all the other nations." Abu Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: this is a hasan hadith.

(A company) is in the nominative case, either as the subject of a nominal sentence or by omitting the predicate of the descriptive particle; its implied meaning is: for the companions of the right hand there are two companies: a company from these and a company from those. The earlier ones are the past nations, and the later ones are this Ummah according to the second view.
