Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: I asked the Prophet ﷺ about His saying: ﴿Indeed We have produced them with a [special] production, and made them virgins, loving, of equal age﴾, and he said: "O Umm Salamah, they are those who died in this world as old women, toothless, with weak eyes and watery eyes; Allah made them, after old age, of equal age, of one birth in uniformity." Al-Nahhas supported it with a chain from Anas, who said: Ahmad ibn 'Amr related to us, saying: 'Amr ibn 'Ali related to us, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us from Musa ibn 'Ubaydah, from Yazid al-Raqashi, from Anas ibn Malik, who raised it: ﴿Indeed We have produced them with a [special] production﴾, he said: "They are the old women, toothless and with watery eyes, who were in this world toothless with watery eyes." Al-Musayyib ibn Sharik said: The Prophet ﷺ said concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed We have produced them with a [special] production﴾ [the verse [[An addition from B.]]], he said: "They are the old women of this world. Allah produces them with a new creation, so that whenever their husbands come to them they find them virgins." When 'A'ishah heard that she said: "Oh, my pain!" So the Prophet ﷺ said to her: "There is no pain there."

(﴿'uruban﴾) is the plural of 'arub. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others said: al-'urub are women who are passionate toward their husbands. Also from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the ʿarūb, the coquettish. 'Ikrimah: the flirtatious. Ibn Zayd: in the dialect of the people of Madinah. From this is the saying of Labid:

"And in the howdah is an 'arub, not indecent, / with buttocks that are full, before whom the eye is dazzled."

It is the shaklah in the dialect of the people of Makkah. Also from Zayd ibn Aslam: the one good in speech. Also from 'Ikrimah and Qatadah: the 'urub are those who show affection to their husbands, and its derivation is from a'rab, meaning to make clear; so the 'arub makes her love for her husband clear by coquetry, flirtation and good speech. It was said: she is the one who is good in obedience (tab'ul), that is, submissive to her husband out of love for him, so that she may be more pleasurable to enjoy. Ja'far ibn Muhammad related from his father from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said concerning ('uruban): "Their speech is Arabic." Hamzah and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited ('urban) with a sukun on the ra'. The rest recited it with a damma, and both are permissible in the plural of fa'ul.

(﴿atraban﴾): of one birth in uniformity and one age of thirty-three years. It is said of women atrab, and of men aqran. The Arabs used to incline toward women who had passed the limit of youth but had not reached old age. It was also said: atraban means equals and similar ones; this was said by Mujahid. Al-Suddi: atrab in character, with no hatred or envy among them. It was said: the wide-eyed maidens are for the foremost, and the atrab, the 'urub, are for the companions of the right hand.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿A company of the earlier generations, and a company of the later ones.﴾ The discourse returns to His words: (And the companions of the right hand — what are the companions of the right hand?) That is, they are (a company of the earlier generations, and a company of the later ones), and the meaning of this has already been discussed.

Abu al-Aliyah, Mujahid, Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and al-Dahhak said: (A company of the earlier generations) means the early ones of this Ummah (and a company of the later ones) means the later ones of this Ummah. What supports this is what was narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding this verse, (A company of the earlier generations, and a company of the later ones), that the Prophet ﷺ said: "They are all from my Ummah."

Al-Wahidi said: the companions of the Garden are of two halves: a half from the past nations and a half from this Ummah. This is refuted by what Ibn Majah related in his Sunan and al-Tirmidhi in his Jami' from Buraydah ibn Khusayb (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The people of Paradise are one hundred and twenty rows; eighty of them are from this Ummah and forty from all the other nations." Abu Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: this is a hasan hadith.

(A company) is in the nominative case, either as the subject of a nominal sentence or by omitting the predicate of the descriptive particle; its implied meaning is: for the companions of the right hand there are two companies: a company from these and a company from those. The earlier ones are the past nations, and the later ones are this Ummah according to the second view.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 41–56:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the companions of the left hand—what are the companions of the left hand?﴾ He mentioned the abodes of the people of the Fire and named them "the companions of the left hand," because they take their books with their left hands. Then He magnified their mention regarding the land and the punishment, saying: (What are the companions of the left hand? In scorching wind and boiling water.) As-samum (the scorching wind) is the hot wind that enters the pores of the body. What is meant here is the heat of the Fire and its scorching blast.

(And boiling water) That is, water whose heat has become extreme. When the Fire burns their livers and bodies, they flee to the boiling water, like one who flees from fire to water to extinguish the heat with it, but he finds it boiling hot, at the extreme of heat and seething. This has already been mentioned in (al-Qital) [[See vol. 16, p. 237.]]: (And they are given boiling water to drink, which cuts their bowels to pieces).

(And a shade of black smoke) That is, they flee from the scorching wind to the shade as the people of this world do, but they find it a shade of black smoke, that is, of the smoke of Hell, intensely black. This is related from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others. Likewise, al-yahmum in the language means the intensely black; it is of the form fa'ul from al-hamm, which is fat blackened by the burning of the fire. It was also said that it is derived from al-hummam, which is charcoal. Ad-Dahhak said: The Fire is black, its people are black, and everything in it is black. It is also related from Ibn Abbas: The Fire is black. Ibn Zayd said: al-yahmum is a mountain in Hell to whose shade the people of the Fire seek refuge.

(Neither cool) but hot, because it is from the smoke of the edge of Hell.

(Nor pleasant) Pleasant and agreeable, related from ad-Dahhak. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: nor is its appearance good, and everything without good in it is not pleasant. It was also said: (And a shade of black smoke) means from the Fire by which they are tormented, like His saying: (For them there will be canopies of fire above them and canopies beneath them) [[See vol. 15, p. 243.]].

(Indeed, they were before that affluent) That is, they only deserved this punishment because in the world they were enjoying themselves through what is forbidden. Al-mutraf is the one given luxury, related from Ibn Abbas and others. As-Suddi said: (affluent) means polytheists.

(And they used to persist in the great violation) That is, they persisted in polytheism, related from al-Hasan, ad-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd. Qatadah and Mujahid said: the great sin from which they did not repent. ash-Sha'bi said: it is the perjury (al-yamin al-ghamus), which is among the major sins. It is said: he broke (hanatha) his oath, meaning he did not fulfil it and was faithless regarding it. They used to swear that there would be no resurrection, and that the idols were rivals of Allah; that was their violation, as Allah the Exalted said, informing about them: (And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that Allah will not resurrect those who die) [[See vol. 10, p. 15.]]. And in the report: he used to engage in tahannuth in Hira, that is, he did what would remove from himself the violation (hinth), which is sin.

(And they used to say: "When we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected?") This is their astonishment at the matter of resurrection and their denial of it. So Allah the Exalted said: (Say) to them, O Muhammad: (Indeed, the former peoples) of your forefathers (and the later ones) of you (will surely be gathered to the appointed time of a known day) meaning the Day of Resurrection. The meaning of the speech is an oath, and the entry of the lam in His saying: (will surely be gathered) is the indicator of the oath in meaning; that is, "you will surely be gathered," an oath of truth contrary to your false oath. (Then indeed you, O astray ones) from guidance, (the deniers) of the resurrection, (will surely eat from a tree of zaqqum), which is a tree of hideous appearance and hideous taste, and it is the one mentioned in Surat as-Saffat [[See vol. 15, p. 85.]].

(Then you will fill your bellies from it) That is, from the tree, because what is meant by the tree is a single tree. It is permissible that the first min be extra, and it is permissible that the object be omitted, as if he said: (will surely eat from a tree of zaqqum) food. His saying: (of zaqqum) is an attribute of tree; when you consider the preposition extra, the attribute is put in the accusative according to meaning, or put in the genitive according to form; but if you consider the object omitted, the attribute is only in a genitive position.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And drink on top of it﴾ That is, on the zaqqum, or on the eating, or on the tree, because it is masculine and feminine.

(Of boiling water) which is water heated to the boil whose seething has become intense, and it is the pus of the people of the Fire; that is, it brings them thirst, so they eat from the zaqqum with extreme hunger and thirst, and they drink water they think will remove the thirst, but they find it boiling hot.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And drink like thirsty camels drinking﴾ The reading of Nafi', 'Asim and Hamzah is (shurb) with a dammed shin. The rest read it with a fatha. Both are good dialects: the Arabs say: shariba shurban and sharban and shirban and shurubun with two dammas. Abu Zayd said: I heard the Arabs say it with damma, fatha and kasra of the shin, and the fatha is the sound verbal noun, because every verbal noun of a triliteral root originally follows the pattern fa'l; do you not see that you reduce it to the single occurrence, saying fa'lah, like sharbah, and with the damma it is the noun. It was also said: the fatha and the noun are both verbal nouns, so sharb is like akl, shurb is like dhikr, and shirb with kasra is the drink that is drunk, like tahn (ground) is the ground grain. Al-Heem are camels that are thirsty and never quenched because of a disease that afflicts them, related from Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, Qatadah, as-Suddi and others. Ikrimah also said: they are sick camels. Ad-Dahhak: al-heem are camels afflicted by a disease from which they become intensely thirsty; its singular is ahyam and the feminine is hayma'. This disease is called al-hiyam. Qays ibn al-Mulawwah said:

It is said: the disease of hiyam has befallen him, and my soul knows the place of its cure.

And a people who are heem also means thirsty, and they have hamu hiyaman. Among the Arabs some say of camels:ha'im and ha'imah, and the plural is hiyam. Labid said:

I passed by their familiar traces with exhausted riders, and emaciated camels from the Idi breed, the heem [[Shu'th: men whose condition was spoiled by hardship and travel. Atlah: emaciated camels, singular talih. Al-Idi: camels attributed to a stallion; it is also said attributed to a people called al-Id.]] [[That is, the ha' was lightened and kasra given for the sake of the ya'.]]

Ad-Dahhak, al-Akhfash, Ibn Uyaynah and Ibn Kaysan said: al-heem is the easy land of sand. It is also related from Ibn Abbas: they drink like the sands that are not quenched by water. al-Mahdawi: it is said of anything not quenched, of camels and sand, that it is ahyam and hayma'. In as-Sihah: al-hiyam with damma is the most intense thirst; al-hiyam is like madness from love. al-hiyam is a disease that seizes camels so that they wander in the land and do not graze. It is said: a hayma' camel. Al-haymaa is also the wasteland with no water in it. Al-hayam with fatha is sand that does not hold together, so that it flows from the hand because of its softness; its plural is hiym, like qadhal and qudhul. Al-hiyam with kasra is thirsty camels; the singular is haymán, and a hayma' camel is like 'atshan and 'atsha.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is their hospitality on the Day of Judgement﴾ That is, their provision prepared for them, like the nuzul (hospitality) prepared for guests as an honour to them, and in it there is mockery, as in His saying: (So give them good tidings of a painful punishment), and like the saying of Abu as-Sa'd ad-Dabbi:

When the tyrant came to us with the army as guests, we made the spears and the sharp swords his hospitality.

Yunus ibn Habib and Abbas on the authority of Abu 'Amr read (this is their nuzul) with sukun on the zay, and the discussion of it has passed at the end of (Al 'Imran) [[See vol. 4, p. 321]].

(On the Day of Judgement) the Day of Recompense, meaning in Hell.

Then He magnified their mention regarding the land and the punishment, saying: (What are the companions of the left hand? In scorching wind and boiling water.) As-samum (the scorching wind) is the hot wind that enters the pores of the body. What is meant here is the heat of the Fire and its scorching blast.

(And boiling water) That is, water whose heat has become extreme. When the Fire burns their livers and bodies, they flee to the boiling water, like one who flees from fire to water to extinguish the heat with it, but he finds it boiling hot, at the extreme of heat and seething. This has already been mentioned in (al-Qital) [[See vol. 16, p. 237.]]: (And they are given boiling water to drink, which cuts their bowels to pieces).

(And a shade of black smoke) That is, they flee from the scorching wind to the shade as the people of this world do, but they find it a shade of black smoke, that is, of the smoke of Hell, intensely black. This is related from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others. Likewise, al-yahmum in the language means the intensely black; it is of the form fa'ul from al-hamm, which is fat blackened by the burning of the fire. It was also said that it is derived from al-hummam, which is charcoal. Ad-Dahhak said: The Fire is black, its people are black, and everything in it is black. It is also related from Ibn Abbas: The Fire is black. Ibn Zayd said: al-yahmum is a mountain in Hell to whose shade the people of the Fire seek refuge.

(Neither cool) but hot, because it is from the smoke of the edge of Hell.

(Nor pleasant) Pleasant and agreeable, related from ad-Dahhak. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: nor is its appearance good, and everything without good in it is not pleasant. It was also said: (And a shade of black smoke) means from the Fire by which they are tormented, like His saying: (For them there will be canopies of fire above them and canopies beneath them) [[See vol. 15, p. 243.]].

(Indeed, they were before that affluent) That is, they only deserved this punishment because in the world they were enjoying themselves through what is forbidden. Al-mutraf is the one given luxury, related from Ibn Abbas and others. As-Suddi said: (affluent) means polytheists.

(And they used to persist in the great violation) That is, they persisted in polytheism, related from al-Hasan, ad-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd. Qatadah and Mujahid said: the great sin from which they did not repent. ash-Sha'bi said: it is the perjury (al-yamin al-ghamus), which is among the major sins. It is said: he broke (hanatha) his oath, meaning he did not fulfil it and was faithless regarding it. They used to swear that there would be no resurrection, and that the idols were rivals of Allah; that was their violation, as Allah the Exalted said, informing about them: (And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that Allah will not resurrect those who die) [[See vol. 10, p. 15.]]. And in the report: he used to engage in tahannuth in Hira, that is, he did what would remove from himself the violation (hinth), which is sin.

(And they used to say: "When we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected?") This is their astonishment at the matter of resurrection and their denial of it. So Allah the Exalted said: (Say) to them, O Muhammad: (Indeed, the former peoples) of your forefathers (and the later ones) of you (will surely be gathered to the appointed time of a known day) meaning the Day of Resurrection. The meaning of the speech is an oath, and the entry of the lam in His saying: (will surely be gathered) is the indicator of the oath in meaning; that is, "you will surely be gathered," an oath of truth contrary to your false oath. (Then indeed you, O astray ones) from guidance, (the deniers) of the resurrection, (will surely eat from a tree of zaqqum), which is a tree of hideous appearance and hideous taste, and it is the one mentioned in Surat as-Saffat [[See vol. 15, p. 85.]].

(Then you will fill your bellies from it) That is, from the tree, because what is meant by the tree is a single tree. It is permissible that the first min be extra, and it is permissible that the object be omitted, as if he said: (will surely eat from a tree of zaqqum) food. His saying: (of zaqqum) is an attribute of tree; when you consider the preposition extra, the attribute is put in the accusative according to meaning, or put in the genitive according to form; but if you consider the object omitted, the attribute is only in a genitive position.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And drink on top of it﴾ That is, on the zaqqum, or on the eating, or on the tree, because it is masculine and feminine.

(Of boiling water) which is water heated to the boil whose seething has become intense, and it is the pus of the people of the Fire; that is, it brings them thirst, so they eat from the zaqqum with extreme hunger and thirst, and they drink water they think will remove the thirst, but they find it boiling hot.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And drink like thirsty camels drinking﴾ The reading of Nafi', 'Asim and Hamzah is (shurb) with a dammed shin. The rest read it with a fatha. Both are good dialects: the Arabs say: shariba shurban and sharban and shirban and shurubun with two dammas. Abu Zayd said: I heard the Arabs say it with damma, fatha and kasra of the shin, and the fatha is the sound verbal noun, because every verbal noun of a triliteral root originally follows the pattern fa'l; do you not see that you reduce it to the single occurrence, saying fa'lah, like sharbah, and with the damma it is the noun. It was also said: the fatha and the noun are both verbal nouns, so sharb is like akl, shurb is like dhikr, and shirb with kasra is the drink that is drunk, like tahn (ground) is the ground grain. Al-Heem are camels that are thirsty and never quenched because of a disease that afflicts them, related from Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, Qatadah, as-Suddi and others. Ikrimah also said: they are sick camels. Ad-Dahhak: al-heem are camels afflicted by a disease from which they become intensely thirsty; its singular is ahyam and the feminine is hayma'. This disease is called al-hiyam. Qays ibn al-Mulawwah said:

It is said: the disease of hiyam has befallen him, and my soul knows the place of its cure.

And a people who are heem also means thirsty, and they have hamu hiyaman. Among the Arabs some say of camels:ha'im and ha'imah, and the plural is hiyam. Labid said:

I passed by their familiar traces with exhausted riders, and emaciated camels from the Idi breed, the heem [[Shu'th: men whose condition was spoiled by hardship and travel. Atlah: emaciated camels, singular talih. Al-Idi: camels attributed to a stallion; it is also said attributed to a people called al-Id.]] [[That is, the ha' was lightened and kasra given for the sake of the ya'.]]

Ad-Dahhak, al-Akhfash, Ibn Uyaynah and Ibn Kaysan said: al-heem is the easy land of sand. It is also related from Ibn Abbas: they drink like the sands that are not quenched by water. al-Mahdawi: it is said of anything not quenched, of camels and sand, that it is ahyam and hayma'. In as-Sihah: al-hiyam with damma is the most intense thirst; al-hiyam is like madness from love. al-hiyam is a disease that seizes camels so that they wander in the land and do not graze. It is said: a hayma' camel. Al-haymaa is also the wasteland with no water in it. Al-hayam with fatha is sand that does not hold together, so that it flows from the hand because of its softness; its plural is hiym, like qadhal and qudhul. Al-hiyam with kasra is thirsty camels; the singular is haymán, and a hayma' camel is like 'atshan and 'atsha.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is their hospitality on the Day of Judgement﴾ That is, their provision prepared for them, like the nuzul (hospitality) prepared for guests as an honour to them, and in it there is mockery, as in His saying: (So give them good tidings of a painful punishment), and like the saying of Abu as-Sa'd ad-Dabbi:

When the tyrant came to us with the army as guests, we made the spears and the sharp swords his hospitality.

Yunus ibn Habib and Abbas on the authority of Abu 'Amr read (this is their nuzul) with sukun on the zay, and the discussion of it has passed at the end of (Al 'Imran) [[See vol. 4, p. 321]].

(On the Day of Judgement) the Day of Recompense, meaning in Hell.

It is said: a hayma' camel. Al-haymaa is also the wasteland with no water in it. Al-hayam with fatha is sand that does not hold together, so that it flows from the hand because of its softness; its plural is hiym, like qadhal and qudhul. Al-hiyam with kasra is thirsty camels; the singular is haymán, and a hayma' camel is like 'atshan and 'atsha.

When the tyrant came to us with the army as guests, we made the spears and the sharp swords his hospitality.

Yunus ibn Habib and Abbas on the authority of Abu 'Amr read (this is their nuzul) with sukun on the zay, and the discussion of it has passed at the end of (Al 'Imran) [[See vol. 4, p. 321]].

(On the Day of Judgement) the Day of Recompense, meaning in Hell.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 57–62:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We created you, so why do you not believe?﴾ That is, why do you not believe in the Resurrection? Because the re-creation is like the initial creation. It has also been said: the meaning is, We created your provision, so why do you not believe that this is your food, if you do not believe? His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you considered the semen that you emit?﴾ That is, what you pour out of the seminal fluid (al-mani) into the wombs of women.

﴿Is it you who create it, or are We the Creator?﴾ That is, do you form the human being from it, or are We the ones who decree and fashion? This is an argument against them and an explanation of the first verse: that is, if you acknowledge that We are its creators and no one else is, then acknowledge the Resurrection. Abu al-Sammal, Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa' and Ashhab al-Uqayli read (tamnūna) with a fatha on the tā', and both are dialects: amnā and manā, amdhā and madhā, yumnī and yamnī, yumdhī and yamdhī. Al-Mawardi said: In my view it is possible that their meanings differ, so amnā is when one ejaculates from intercourse, and manā is when one ejaculates from a wet dream. Regarding the naming of the semen as manī (mani), there are two views: one is that it is named for its emission (imnā'uhu), which is its spilling; the second is that it is named for its measuring (taqdīr), and from this comes al-manā, by which things are weighed, because it is a measure for that; likewise, the manī is a sound measure for the shaping of creation.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We have decreed death among you﴾ is also an argument: the One who is able to cause death is able to create, and whoever is able to create is able to resurrect. Mujahid, Humayd, Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn Kathir read (qaddarnā) with a light dal. The rest read it with a shadda. Al-Dahhak said: that is, We made it equal among the people of the heavens and the people of the earth. It has also been said: We decreed. It has also been said: We wrote. The meanings are close, and no one remains except Him, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿And We are not outstripped, in order to replace your likenesses﴾: that is, if We wish to replace your likenesses, no one can precede Us, meaning, no one can overcome Us.

﴿And We are not outstripped﴾ means: not overcome. Al-Tabari said: the meaning is, We decreed death among you, so that after your death We replace you with others of your kind, and We are not outstripped regarding your terms (ājāl), meaning no one who is late comes forward and no one who is early is delayed.

﴿And We will bring you into being in what you do not know﴾ regarding forms and shapes. Al-Hasan said: that is, We will make you apes and swine, as We did with peoples before you. It has also been said: the meaning is, We will bring you into being in the Resurrection in forms other than your forms in this world, so the believer is beautified by the whiteness of his face, and the disbeliever is made ugly by the blackness of his face. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: that is, in the crops of black birds that are in Barahut, as if they were swallows, and Barahut is a valley in Yemen. Mujahid said: ﴿in what you do not know﴾ means in whatever creation We wish. It has also been said: the meaning is, We will bring you into being in a world you do not know, and in a place you do not know.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you have certainly known the first creation﴾: that is, when you were created from a drop, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, and you were nothing, according to Mujahid and others. Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: it means the creation of Adam, peace be upon him.

﴿Then why do you not remember?﴾ That is, why do you not remember? In a report: "How wondrous, how utterly wondrous, is the one who denies the second creation while he sees the first creation, and how wondrous is the one who believes in the final creation while he does not strive for the abode of permanence." The common reading is (al-nash'a) with a short vowel. Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (al-nash'ā'a) with a long vowel, and its explanation has passed in (al-'Ankabut) [see vol. 13, p. 337].

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 56, verses 68–74:

Allah's statement: ﴿Have you considered the water that you drink?﴾ So that you may give life to yourselves by it, and quench your thirst with it, because drink is only a follower of food. This is why food was mentioned first in the verse before it. Do you not see that you give your guest drink after you have fed him?

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you reversed it, you would fall under the verse of Abu al-'Ala':

When the guests of people are given pure milk to drink, they give their guests cold, sweet water [[al-mahd: pure milk; shabam: cold water.]]

Some of the Arabs were given a drink and said: "I do not drink except on a full stomach" [[thamila: a full stomach of fodder or food.]].

﴿Is it you who sent it down from the clouds (al-muzn)?﴾ That is, from the clouds. Its singular is muznah. The poet said:

So we are like the water of the clouds: in our origin there is no dullness, and among us there is no stingy person [[nasab: origin of anything. A man who is kaham or kahim is heavy, of no use.]].

This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others: al-muzn means the clouds. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Thawri that al-muzn means the sky and the clouds. In al-Sihah, Abu Zayd said: al-muznah is a white cloud, and its plural is muzn. Al-muznah also means a single rainfall. He said:

Do you not see that Allah sent down a muznah, while the wild cows in their hiding places were moving their heads [[This line is by Aws ibn Hajr. Tuqamma'u: they shake their heads to drive away the qam'ah, a blue fly that enters the noses of animals.]]?

﴿Or are We the ones who send it down?﴾ That is: since you know that I sent it down, why do you not thank Me by sincerely worshipping Me? And why do you deny My power to restore?

﴿If We willed, We would make it salty (ujaj)﴾ That is, extremely salty, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Al-Hasan said: bitter and foul, from which you benefit neither in drinking, nor in farming, nor in anything else.

﴿Why then do you not give thanks?﴾ That is: why do you not thank the One who did this for you?

Allah's statement: ﴿Have you considered the fire that you kindle?﴾ That is: tell Me about the fire that you produce by striking green wood [[Ibn al-Shajar and other dialect variants are not relevant here.]]

﴿Is it you who grew its tree?﴾ That is, the trees from which the firestarter (al-zinad) is made, which are al-markh and al-'affar. From this comes their saying: "In every tree there is fire," and "al-markh and al-'affar have become glorious (istamjada)," meaning they have taken much of it, as if they took from the fire what was enough for them. It is also said that they quickly produce sparks. It is said: awrayt al-nar, when you struck the fire. And waraya al-zind yari, when the fire sparked from it. There is another dialect: wariya al-zind yari, with kasra in both.

﴿Or are We the producers?﴾ That is, the originators and creators. That is: since you know My power, thank Me, and do not deny My power to resurrect.

Allah's statement: ﴿We have made it a reminder﴾ That is, the fire of this world is a reminder of the great fire, as Qatada said. Mujahid said: a means of illumination for people in the darkness. It is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Your fire which the children of Adam kindle is one part out of seventy parts of the fire of Hell." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, indeed it would be sufficient." He said: "It has been made superior to it by sixty-nine parts, each of which is like its heat."

﴿And a provision for the wayfarers (lil-muqwin)﴾ Al-Dahhak said: that is, a benefit for travelers, who are called such because they stop in al-qiyy, which is the barren land with nothing in it. Al-Farra' said: travelers are called muqwin when they stop in al-qiyy, which is the barren land with nothing in it. Likewise al-qawa and al-qawa', with madd and qasr, and a manzil qawa' is one with no one in it. It is said: aqwat al-dar and qawiyat as well, meaning it became empty of its inhabitants. Al-Nabigha said:

O abode of Mayyah in al-'Aliya and al-Sanad, it has become empty, and long ages have passed over it.

And 'Antara said:

Greetings to a campsite whose traces have grown old, emptied and barren after Umm al-Haytham.

It is also said: aqwa means qawiya, and qawiya means his companions became strong. Aqwa means he traveled, that is, he stopped in the qawa' and the qiyy. Mujahid said: (lil-muqwin) means those who benefit from it among all people, in cooking, baking, warming themselves, and lighting. It reminds them of the fire of Hell, so they seek refuge in Allah from it. Ibn Zayd said: for the hungry, in preparing their food. It is said: aqwaytu mundhu kadha wa kadha, meaning I have not eaten anything. And so-and-so spent the night qawa', and spent the night qafr, when he spent the night hungry without food. The poet, who is Hatim al-Ta'i, said:

Indeed I choose to be hungry in the stomach, guarding against being called stingy.

Al-Rabi' and al-Suddi said: (al-muqwin) means those who stop and have no firestarter with them. That is, a fire by which they could light and bake. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. Qutrub said: al-muqwi is one of the words with opposite meanings: it can mean poor, and it can mean rich. It is said: aqwa al-rajul when he has no provisions, and aqwa when his animals are strong and his wealth is abundant. Al-Mahdawi said: the verse is suitable for all of these, because the traveler and the resident, the rich and the poor, all need fire. Al-Tha'labi related that most of the commentators hold the first view. Al-Qushayri said: He specified the traveler for benefit from it because his benefit from it is greater than that of the resident, since people of the desert must have fire, which they light at night so that predators flee from them, and for many of their needs.

Allah's statement: ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ That is: exalt Allah above what the polytheists attribute to Him of rivals and of inability to resurrect.

It is also said: aqwa means qawiya, and qawiya means his companions became strong. Aqwa means he traveled, that is, he stopped in the qawa' and the qiyy. Mujahid said: (lil-muqwin) means those who benefit from it among all people, in cooking, baking, warming themselves, and lighting. It reminds them of the fire of Hell, so they seek refuge in Allah from it. Ibn Zayd said: for the hungry, in preparing their food. It is said: aqwaytu mundhu kadha wa kadha, meaning I have not eaten anything. And so-and-so spent the night qawa', and spent the night qafr, when he spent the night hungry without food. The poet, who is Hatim al-Ta'i, said:

Indeed I choose to be hungry in the stomach, guarding against being called stingy.

Al-Rabi' and al-Suddi said: (al-muqwin) means those who stop and have no firestarter with them. That is, a fire by which they could light and bake. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. Qutrub said: al-muqwi is one of the words with opposite meanings: it can mean poor, and it can mean rich. It is said: aqwa al-rajul when he has no provisions, and aqwa when his animals are strong and his wealth is abundant. Al-Mahdawi said: the verse is suitable for all of these, because the traveler and the resident, the rich and the poor, all need fire. Al-Tha'labi related that most of the commentators hold the first view. Al-Qushayri said: He specified the traveler for benefit from it because his benefit from it is greater than that of the resident, since people of the desert must have fire, which they light at night so that predators flee from them, and for many of their needs.

Allah's statement: ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ That is: exalt Allah above what the polytheists attribute to Him of rivals and of inability to resurrect.

**Fihi sab' masa'il** (There are seven issues in it.)

**The first issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: (So I do not swear) (*fa-la*). In the view of most exegetes (*mufassirun*), *fa-la* is a redundant particle (*silah*), and the meaning is *fa-uqsimu* (so I swear). The evidence is His saying: (And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you only knew) (56:76). Al-Farra' said: *la* is a negation, and the meaning is "The matter is not as you say," and then *uqsimu* (I swear) begins a new sentence. A man may say, "No, by God, it was not so," without intending to negate an oath. He intends to negate a statement that preceded it, meaning, "The matter is not as you have described, but rather it is such-and-such." It has also been said that *fa-la* means *ala*, used for alerting, as the poet said [the line is by Imru' al-Qays, and its completion is: "And will the one who lived in the past age ever enjoy it again?"]:

*"Ala 'imm sabahan ayyuha al-talalu al-bali"*
("Ah, greet the morning, O ruined abode!")

By this he alerts the listeners to the excellence of the Qur'an, so that they will reflect upon it, and that it is neither poetry, nor magic, nor soothsaying, as they claimed.

Al-Hasan, Humayd and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read (*fa-la-uqsimu*) without an *alif* after the *lam*, as a definite form, and it is a present-tense verb (*fi'l hal*) with an omitted subject (*mubtada'*) to be understood. The sense is: "So indeed I, I swear by that." If it were intended for the future, the *nun* would have been required, and the omission of the *nun* with a verb intended for the future is irregular (*shadh*).

'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: their stations (*manazil*). Al-Hasan said: their dispersal and scattering on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Dahhak said: they are the *anwa'* (star-risings) which the people of the Jahiliyyah used to mention; when they were rained upon they would say, "We have been given rain by the *nw'* of such-and-such."

Al-Mawardi: His saying, Exalted is He, (So I do not swear) may be used in its literal sense of negating an oath.

Al-Qushayri: It is an oath. God, Exalted is He, may swear by whatever He wills, but it is not for us to swear by other than God, Exalted is He, or by His eternal attributes.

I [al-Qurtubi] say: This is indicated by the reading of al-Hasan (*fa-la'uqsimu*), and by the things by which He, glorified is He, swore from among His creatures in more than one place in His Book.

Ibn 'Abbas said: What is meant by *mawaqi' al-nujum* is the revelation of the Qur'an in installments (*nujuman*). God, Exalted is He, sent it down from the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*) in the highest heaven to the noble scribes (*al-safara al-kiram*); the scribes then delivered it in installments to Jibril over twenty nights, and Jibril delivered it in installments to Muhammad (ﷺ) over twenty years. So He sends it down upon the events of His community. Al-Mawardi related this from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi.

Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: Ismail ibn Ishaq al-Qadi narrated to us, Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal narrated to us, Hammam narrated to us, from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Qur'an was sent down to the lowest heaven all at once, then it was sent down to the earth in installments. After that it was divided into groups of five verses, five verses, and fewer or more. This is the saying of God, Exalted is He: (So I do not swear by the positions of the stars. And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you only knew. Indeed it is a noble Qur'an) (56:75–77)."

Al-Farra' related from Ibn Mas'ud that *mawaqi' al-nujum* is the clear (*muhkam*) Qur'an.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (*bi-mawqi'*) in the singular. This is the reading of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, al-Nakha'i, al-A'mash, Ibn Muhaysin and Ruways from Ya'qub. The rest read it in the plural. Whoever reads it in the singular does so because it is a collective noun (*ism jins*), in which the singular stands for the plural. Whoever reads it in the plural does so because of the variety of its kinds.

It has been said that the pronoun (*ha'*, "it") refers to the Qur'an, meaning, "Indeed the Qur'an is a mighty oath," as Ibn 'Abbas and others said. It has also been said that what God swore by is great, and (Indeed it is a noble Qur'an) mentions the thing sworn to. That is: "I swear by the positions of the stars that this Qur'an is a noble Qur'an, not magic, nor soothsaying, nor fabrication, but rather a noble and praiseworthy Qur'an, which God made a miracle (*mu'jizah*) for His Prophet (ﷺ). It is noble to the believers, because it is the speech of their Lord and a healing for their hearts, and it is noble to the people of heaven, because it is the revelation (*tanzil*) and inspiration of their Lord."

It has been said: (*karim*) means uncreated. It has been said: (*karim*) because of the noble morals and meanings it contains. It has been said: because whoever memorizes it is honored, and whoever recites it is revered.

**The fourth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: (In a Book kept hidden) (56:78). It means guarded (*masun*) with God, Exalted is He. It has been said: *maknun* means protected from falsehood. The Book here is a book in heaven, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Jabir ibn Zayd and Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is the Preserved Tablet. 'Ikrimah said: it is the Torah and the Gospel, in which there is mention of the Qur'an and of the one to whom it was sent down. Al-Suddi said: it is the Psalms (*Zabur*). Mujahid and Qatadah said: it is the codex (*mushaf*) that is in our hands.

Anas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: None touch that Book except those purified from sins, and they are the angels. Likewise Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibn Zayd said: they are those who have been purified from sins, like the messenger angels and the messengers from among the children of Adam. Jibril, who brings it down, is purified, and the messengers to whom he brings it are purified. Al-Kalbi said: they are the noble, righteous scribes (*al-safara al-kiram al-barara*). All of this is one view, and it is similar to what Malik chose when he said: "The best I have heard concerning His saying, (None touch it except the purified), is that it is like the verse in (*'Abasa wa-tawalla*) [surah 80]: 'Who will remember it? In honored scrolls, exalted, purified, in the hands of scribes, noble and righteous'" (80:12–16).

[Reference: vol. 19, p. 213.] He means that the purified are the angels who were described with purity in Surah 'Abasa. It has been said: the meaning of (*la yamassuhu*, "none touch it") is: none bring it down (*la yanzilu bihi*) except the purified (*al-mutahharun*), meaning the messenger angels bringing it to the messengers among the prophets. It has been said: none touch the Preserved Tablet, which is the Hidden Book, except the purified angels. It has been said: Israfil is the one entrusted with that, as al-Qushayri related. Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is false, because the angels cannot reach it at any time nor arrive at it in any state; and if this were the meaning, there would be no room for the exception. As for the one who said it is what is in the hands of the angels in the scrolls, that is a probable view, and it is the choice of Malik. It has also been said: the intended *kitab* is the codex in our hands, and this is the most apparent.

Malik and others narrated that the letter of 'Amr ibn Hazm, which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) wrote to him, reads: "From Muhammad the Prophet to Shurahbil ibn 'Abd Kulal, al-Harith ibn 'Abd Kulal, and Nu'aym ibn 'Abd Kulal, the chiefs of Dhu Ru'ayn, Ma'afir and Hamdan. Now then..." And in his letter was: "None should touch the Qur'an except one who is pure (*tahir*)."

Ibn 'Umar said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not touch the Qur'an unless you are pure."

'Umar's sister said to 'Umar when he came to her house upon his conversion and she had asked for the codex: "(None touch it except the purified)." He stood up, washed, and embraced Islam. This has already passed at the beginning of Surah Ta-Ha [vol. 11, p. 163].

On this meaning, Qatadah and others said: (None touch it except the purified) from minor and major impurity (*al-ahdath wa-al-anjas*). Al-Kalbi said: from polytheism (*shirk*). Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: from sins and wrongdoings. It has also been said: the meaning of (*la yamassuhu*, "none touch it") is: none recite it (*la yaqra'uhu*) except the purified, meaning the monotheists (*al-muwahhidun*). This was said by Muhammad ibn Fudayl and 'Abdah.

'Ikrimah said: Ibn 'Abbas used to forbid any Jew or Christian from being allowed to recite the Qur'an.

Al-Farra' said: None find its taste, its benefit, and its blessing except the purified, that is, the believers in the Qur'an.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is the choice of al-Bukhari, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is pleased with God as Lord, Islam as religion, and Muhammad (ﷺ) as Prophet, has tasted the flavor of faith."

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: Its interpretation and its explanation are known only to one whom God has purified from polytheism and hypocrisy.

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: None are granted success in acting upon it except the fortunate.

It has been said: the meaning is that none touch its reward except the believers. Mu'adh related this from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Then it has been said: the apparent meaning of the verse is a report about the Law (*shar'*), meaning none touch it except the purified according to the Law. If something contrary to this is found, it is outside the Law. This is the choice of al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi, who rejected the view that its wording is that of a report while its meaning is a command.

This meaning has already passed in Surah al-Baqarah [vol. 3, p. 91].

Al-Mahdawi said: It is permissible that it be a command, and the *damma* on the *sin* would then be an inflectional *damma* (*dammat i'rab*, a vowel marking grammatical case). It is also permissible that it be a prohibition, and the *damma* on the *sin* would then be a built-in *damma* (*dammat bina'*, a fixed vowel), and the verb would be in the jussive mood (*majzum*).

**The sixth issue:** Scholars differed over touching the codex without ritual ablution (*wudu'*). The majority hold that it is prohibited to touch it because of the hadith of 'Amr ibn Hazm. This is the view of 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Sa'id ibn Zayd, 'Ata', al-Zuhri, al-Nakha'i, al-Hakam and Hammad, and a group of jurists including Malik and al-Shafi'i.

It has been related from al-Hakam, Hammad and Dawud ibn 'Ali that there is no harm in carrying it and touching it for a Muslim or a disbeliever, whether pure or impure, except that Dawud said: It is not permissible for a polytheist to carry it.

They (those who permit it) argued for this permission with the Prophet's (ﷺ) letter to Caesar, but that was a case of necessity (*darurah*), so there is no proof in it.

**The seventh issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: (A revelation from the Lord of the worlds) (56:80). That is, *munazzal* (sent down), like the saying "the striking of the commander" and "the weaving of Yemen" (verbal nouns used in the sense of the object). It has been said: (*tanzil*, "revelation") is an adjective of His saying, Exalted is He: (Indeed it is a noble Qur'an). It has also been said: that is, it is a revelation.

("Ah, greet the morning, O ruined abode!")

If it were intended for the future, the *nun* would have been required, and the omission of the *nun* with a verb intended for the future is irregular (*shadh*).

**The second issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: (by the positions of the stars). *Mawaqi' al-nujum* means their setting places and their places of setting, according to Qatadah and others. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: their stations (*manazil*). Al-Hasan said: their dispersal and scattering on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Dahhak said: they are the *anwa'* (star-risings) which the people of the Jahiliyyah used to mention; when they were rained upon they would say, "We have been given rain by the *nw'* of such-and-such."

Al-Mawardi: His saying, Exalted is He, (So I do not swear) may be used in its literal sense of negating an oath.

Al-Qushayri: It is an oath. God, Exalted is He, may swear by whatever He wills, but it is not for us to swear by other than God, Exalted is He, or by His eternal attributes.

I [al-Qurtubi] say: This is indicated by the reading of al-Hasan (*fa-la'uqsimu*), and by the things by which He, glorified is He, swore from among His creatures in more than one place in His Book.

God, Exalted is He, sent it down from the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*) in the highest heaven to the noble scribes (*al-safara al-kiram*); the scribes then delivered it in installments to Jibril over twenty nights, and Jibril delivered it in installments to Muhammad (ﷺ) over twenty years. Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: Ismail ibn Ishaq al-Qadi narrated to us, Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal narrated to us, Hammam narrated to us, from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Qur'an was sent down to the lowest heaven all at once, then it was sent down to the earth in installments. Al-Farra' related from Ibn Mas'ud that *mawaqi' al-nujum* is the clear (*muhkam*) Qur'an.

Whoever reads it in the singular does so because it is a collective noun (*ism jins*), in which the singular stands for the plural. Whoever reads it in the plural does so because of the variety of its kinds.

It has been said that the pronoun (*ha'*, "it") refers to the Qur'an, meaning, "Indeed the Qur'an is a mighty oath," as Ibn 'Abbas and others said. It has also been said that what God swore by is great, and (Indeed it is a noble Qur'an) mentions the thing sworn to. It has been said: (*karim*) means uncreated. It has been said: (*karim*) because of the noble morals and meanings it contains. It has been said: because whoever memorizes it is honored, and whoever recites it is revered.

**The fourth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: (In a Book kept hidden) (56:78). It means guarded (*masun*) with God, Exalted is He. It has been said: *maknun* means protected from falsehood. 'Ikrimah said: it is the Torah and the Gospel, in which there is mention of the Qur'an and of the one to whom it was sent down. Al-Suddi said: it is the Psalms (*Zabur*). Mujahid and Qatadah said: it is the codex (*mushaf*) that is in our hands.

Anas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: None touch that Book except those purified from sins, and they are the angels. Likewise Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibn Zayd said: they are those who have been purified from sins, like the messenger angels and the messengers from among the children of Adam. Jibril, who brings it down, is purified, and the messengers to whom he brings it are purified. Al-Kalbi said: they are the noble, righteous scribes (*al-safara al-kiram al-barara*). It has been said: the meaning of (*la yamassuhu*, "none touch it") is: none bring it down (*la yanzilu bihi*) except the purified (*al-mutahharun*), meaning the messenger angels bringing it to the messengers among the prophets. Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is false, because the angels cannot reach it at any time nor arrive at it in any state; and if this were the meaning, there would be no room for the exception. As for the one who said it is what is in the hands of the angels in the scrolls, that is a probable view, and it is the choice of Malik. It has also been said: the intended *kitab* is the codex in our hands, and this is the most apparent.

Malik and others narrated that the letter of 'Amr ibn Hazm, which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) wrote to him, reads: "From Muhammad the Prophet to Shurahbil ibn 'Abd Kulal, al-Harith ibn 'Abd Kulal, and Nu'aym ibn 'Abd Kulal, the chiefs of Dhu Ru'ayn, Ma'afir and Hamdan. Ibn 'Umar said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not touch the Qur'an unless you are pure."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 56, verses 81–87:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is it then at this discourse that you scoff?﴾ "This discourse" means the Quran. (You are scoffing) means "you are denying," as said by Ibn Abbas, Ata, and others. The *mudhin* (scoffer) is one whose outward appearance differs from his inner reality, as if he were compared to oil (*duhn*) because of the smoothness of its surface. Muqatil ibn Sulayman and Qatadah said: "Mudhinun" means "disbelievers." A parallel is the verse: ﴿They wish that you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [see vol. 18, p. 230]. Al-Mu'arrij said: the *mudhin* is the hypocrite or the disbeliever who softens his side in order to conceal his disbelief. *Al-idhan* and *al-mudahanah* mean denial, disbelief, and hypocrisy, and their root meaning is softness, and concealing the opposite of what one displays. Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat said:

"Resolve and strength are better than compromise (*al-idhan*), and than incapacity and greed."

*Adhana* and *dahana* have the same meaning. Some said: *dahantu* means "I concealed," and *adhantu* means "I deceived." Al-Dahhak said: "mudhinun" means "turning away." The second aspect is that one believes that Allah sends down water by means of the *nawʾ*, and that it is a cause of the water as Allah has decreed and as it was foreknown in His knowledge. Although this is a permissible view, it also involves disbelief in the blessing of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and ignorance of His subtle wisdom in that He sends down water whenever He wills, sometimes by one *nawʾ* and sometimes by another. Often the *nawʾ* passes without any water descending with it, and that is from Allah, Exalted is He, not from the *nawʾ*.

Likewise Abu Hurayrah used to say, when he woke up to find it had rained: "We were given rain by the *nawʾ* of al-Fath," and then he recited: ﴿Whatever mercy Allah opens to the people, none can withhold it﴾ [see vol. 14, p. 321]. Abu Umar said: This, in my view, is similar to the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "We were given rain by the grace of Allah and His mercy."

Of this same category is the saying of Umar ibn al-Khattab to al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib when he sought rain through him: "O uncle of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), how much of the *nawʾ* of the Pleiades (al-Thurayya) remains?" Al-Abbas said: "The astronomers claim that it crosses the horizon for seven nights after it sets." Before the seventh night had passed, they were given rain. Umar said: "Praise be to Allah, this is by the grace of Allah and His mercy." Umar, may Allah have mercy on him, knew that the *nawʾ* of the Pleiades is a time in which rain is hoped for and expected, so he asked him about it: "Has it passed, or is some of it still remaining?"

Sufyan ibn Uyaynah related from Isma'il ibn Umayyah that the Prophet (ﷺ) heard a man, during one of his journeys, saying, "We were given rain by some of the *athani* of al-Asad (a star-mansion)." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You lie, rather it is the watering of Allah, Mighty and Majestic." Sufyan said: *Athani al-Asad* are the forearm and the forehead.

The common reading is ﴿tukadhdhibun﴾, from *al-takdhib* (denial). Al-Mufaddal, from Asim, and Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿takdhibun﴾ with a fatha on the *ta'* and without the doubling. Its meaning is what we mentioned earlier from the saying of those who said, "We were given rain by the *nawʾ* of such-and-such."

It is established in the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Three things will not cease among my community: boasting about lineages, wailing, and the *anwa'*." The wording of Muslim in this is: "Four things among my community are from the matters of the Jahiliyyah, and they will not abandon them: boasting about ancestry, attacking lineages, seeking rain by the stars, and wailing."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Why then, when it [the soul] reaches the throat﴾, meaning: why not, when the soul or the spirit reaches the throat? There was no prior mention of it, because the meaning is known. Hatim said:

"O Ummi, wealth does not avail a man when the death-rattle takes him one day and his chest constricts."

In a hadith: "The Angel of Death has assistants who cut through the veins and gather the spirit bit by bit until it reaches the throat, and then the Angel of Death takes it."

﴿And you, at that time, are looking on﴾, meaning at My command and My power. It was also said: you are looking at the dying person and cannot do anything for him. Ibn Abbas said: It means that those present among the family of the dead person are waiting to see when his soul will leave. Then it was said: this is a rebuttal of their saying to their brothers: ﴿If they had been with us, they would not have died or been killed﴾ [see vol. 4, p. 246], meaning: Did they restore the spirit of one of them when it reached the throat? It was also said: the meaning is: why not, when the soul of one of you reaches the throat at the time of death, and you are present, holding back his spirit in his body, despite your eagerness for the lengthening of his life and your love for his survival. This is a rebuttal of their saying: ﴿We die and we live, and nothing destroys us but time﴾ [see vol. 16, p. 170]. It was also said: this is addressed to the one who is dying: if what is upon you is not from Allah, why did you not keep your spirit for yourself?

﴿And We are nearer to him than you﴾, meaning in power, knowledge, and sight. Amir ibn Abd al-Qays said: "I never looked at anything without seeing Allah, Exalted is He, nearer to me than it." It was also said: He meant that Our messengers, who take charge of seizing him, are ﴿nearer to him than you﴾, ﴿but you do not see﴾, meaning you do not see them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Why then, if you are not to be held to account?﴾, meaning: why not, if you are not to be called to account and not to be recompensed for your deeds? From this is His saying: ﴿Indeed we are to be held accountable﴾, meaning recompensed and called to account. This has already been mentioned [see vol. 15, p. 82]. It was also said: not owned and not subdued. Al-Farra' and others said: *dantuhu* means "I possessed him." He cited al-Hutay'ah:

"You have indeed governed the affairs of your sons, until you left them finer than flour."

Meaning: you were made their master. *Dana-hu* also means he humbled him and enslaved him, as one says: "I subjugated him and he submitted." This has already been discussed at the opening surah (*al-Fatihah*), in the commentary on His saying: ﴿the Day of Judgment﴾.

﴿You would bring it back﴾, meaning you would return the spirit to the body.

﴿If you are truthful﴾, meaning: and you will never bring it back, so your claim that you are not owned and not held to account is void. The two conditionals ﴿Why then, when it reaches the throat﴾ and ﴿Why then, if you are not to be held to account﴾ are answered by one answer, ﴿you would bring it back﴾, as al-Farra' said. The Arabs sometimes repeat two particles with the same meaning, and among this is His saying: ﴿If guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance, no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾ [see vol. 1, p. 327]. Both conditionals are answered by one answer, though they are two conditions. It was also said: one of them is omitted because the other indicates it. It was also said: there is an inversion of order in these verses, and its sense is: "Why then, and why not, if you are not to be held to account, would you bring it back, returning the soul of this dead person to his body when it has reached the throat?"

The Almighty said: ﴿But if he is among those brought near﴾. He mentioned the classes of creation at death and at resurrection, and explained their ranks, saying: "(But if he is) this one who has died (among those brought near)," and they are the foremost.

(Then rest and provision and a Garden of pleasure.) The common reading is (fa-rawhun) with a fatha on the rā’, and its meaning according to Ibn ʿAbbas and others is: relief from the world. Al-Hasan said: al-rawḥ is mercy. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: al-rawḥ is rest. al-Qutabī said: the meaning is that in the grave there is a pleasant breeze for him. Abu al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAṭāʾ said: al-rawḥ is looking at the Face of God, and al-rayḥān is listening to His speech and His revelation. (And a Garden of pleasure) is that he will not be veiled in it from Almighty God. Al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, al-Jaḥdarī, Ruways and Zayd, from Yaʿqūb, read (furūḥun) with a ḍammah on the rā’, and it is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Ḥasan said: al-rūḥ is mercy, because it is like life to the one who is shown mercy. ʿĀʾishah, may God be pleased with her, said: the Prophet (ﷺ) recited (furūḥun) with a ḍammah on the rā’, and its meaning is: then remaining and life in Paradise, and this is mercy.

(And rayḥān) Mujāhid and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: that is provision. Muqātil said: it is provision in the language of Ḥimyar; one says: "I went out seeking the rayḥān of God," meaning His provision. al-Namir ibn Tawlab said:

"The peace of God and His rayḥān,
and His mercy and abundant rain."

Qatādah said: it is Paradise. al-Ḍaḥḥāk: mercy. It was also said that it is the well-known fragrant basil that is smelled. This was said by al-Ḥasan and also by Qatādah. al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym: this is at death, and Paradise is hidden for him until he is resurrected. Abu al-Jawzāʾ: this is at the taking of his soul; he is received with bunches of rayḥān. Abu al-ʿĀliyah: no one among those brought near in this world departs his soul until two sprigs of rayḥān are brought to him, and he smells them, and then his soul is taken within them. The origin of rayḥān and its derivation was discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Raḥmān [[See p. 157 of this part.]], so reflect on it. Al-Thaʿlabī also set out many sayings on al-rawḥ and al-rayḥān beyond what we have mentioned; whoever wants them will find them there.

The Almighty said: ﴿And if he is among the companions of the right﴾. That is, (if) this one who has died (is among the companions of the right), (then peace be upon you from the companions of the right). That is, you will see from them only what you love of safety, so do not be concerned for them, for they will be safe from the punishment of God. It was also said: the meaning is "peace upon you from them", that is, you are safe from grief over them. The meaning is one. It was also said: that is, the companions of the right will invoke blessings on you, O Muhammad, that God send prayers and peace upon you. It was also said: the meaning is that they will greet you, O Muhammad. It was also said: the meaning is: "You are safe, O servant, from what you dislike, for you are among the companions of the right," so "innaka" is omitted. It was also said: he is greeted with peace in honor. Accordingly, concerning the place of the peace there are three opinions. The first: at the taking of his soul in this world, the angel of death greets him with peace; this was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk. Ibn Masʿūd said: when the angel of death comes to take the soul of the believer, he says: "Your Lord sends you His greetings." This has already passed in Surat al-Naḥl [[See vol. 10, p. 101]] at the Almighty's words: ﴿those whom the angels take in death while they are pure﴾. The second: at his questioning in the grave, Munkar and Nakīr greet him with peace. The third: at his resurrection on the Day of Resurrection, the angels greet him with peace before he reaches them.

I say: It is possible that he is greeted in all three situations, and that this is honor upon honor. And God knows best. According to al-Mubarrad, the answer to (in) is omitted; the estimate is: "Whatever may be of something, (then peace be upon you from the companions of the right) if he is among the companions of the right (then peace be upon you from the companions of the right)." So the answer to the condition is omitted because what precedes it indicates it, just as the answer is omitted in such an expression as "You are a wrongdoer if you do it," because of what precedes it. The view of al-Akhfash is that the fāʾ is the answer to both (amma) and (in), and the meaning of that is: the fāʾ is the answer to (amma), and it has taken the place of the answer to (in) under the estimate mentioned above, and the fāʾ serves as an answer to both on this principle. According to al-Zajjāj, the meaning of (amma) is moving from one thing to another, that is: leave what we were in and take up something else.

The Almighty said: ﴿And if he is among the deniers, the astray﴾: those who deny resurrection, who are astray from guidance and the path of truth. ﴿Then, a welcome of boiling water﴾: that is, for them is provision of boiling water, as He said: ﴿Then indeed you, O astray deniers, will be eating﴾ [[see]] and as He said: ﴿Then indeed for them upon it is a mixture of boiling water﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 87]]. ﴿And burning in Hellfire﴾: entry into the Fire. It was also said: remaining in the Hellfire and suffering the various kinds of its torment. One says: "He roasted him in the fire," meaning he made him burn in it, and here the verbal noun is attributed to its object, as one says: "For so-and-so is the giving of wealth," meaning wealth is given. It was read (wa-taṣliyata) with a kasra on the tāʾ, meaning: "and a welcome from the burning of Hellfire." Then Abu ʿAmr assimilated the tāʾ into the jīm, and this is far-fetched.

﴿Indeed, this is the true certainty﴾: that is, what We have related is the pure certainty and its essence. It is permissible to attribute "truth" to "certainty", though they are the same, because their wording differs. Al-Mubarrad said: it is like your saying "the eye of certainty" and "the pure certainty", so it is of the type of attributing a thing to itself according to the Kufans. According to the Basrans, the truth of the matter is "the certainty" or "the certain report". It was also said: it is emphasis. It was also said: originally "certainty" should be a qualifier of "truth", so the qualified was attributed to the qualifier by extension and metaphor, as in His saying: ﴿and the home of the Hereafter﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 275]]. Qatādah said concerning this verse: God does not leave anyone among people without making him stand before certainty concerning this Qur'an. As for the believer, he attains certainty in this world, and that benefits him on the Day of Resurrection; as for the disbeliever, he attains certainty on the Day of Resurrection when certainty no longer benefits him.

﴿So exalt by the name of your Lord, the Most Great﴾: that is, glorify God, the Exalted, above evil. The "bā’" is extra: that is, glorify the name of your Lord, and the named. It was also said: (fa-sabbiḥ) means: pray by remembering your Lord and by His command. It was also said: mention the name of your Most Great Lord and glorify Him. It is narrated from ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir that he said: when ﴿So exalt by the name of your Lord, the Most Great﴾ was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Put it in your bowing."
